utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Today is my second and final opportunity to address you directly regarding the evidence of this case. Before I begin, I would like to tell you a little bit about the structure of my closing remarks to you. I will not reiterate all of the points raised in the Prosecution final trial brief. That was a public document and contains most of the relevant points the Prosecution requests that you consider. I will touch upon the most important ones and go into greater detail about some points not directly dealt with in that brief. Before I finish my concluding remarks, I will pause, and if the Court has any questions for the Prosecution, I would be happy to attempt to answer them at that point in time, and I will then make some brief closing remarks before finishing. At the outset, I'd like to thank my colleagues, Frederic Ossogo, Sabine Bauer, Yves Roy, Ib Jul Hansen, and David Bruff for their hard work and contribution. My remarks concern both the killing of the five men by the Drina on the 7th of June, which I will refer to as "the Drina River killings." I will also be talking about the over 66 people who died in the Omeragic house on Pionirska Street on the 14th of June. I will refer to that case as "the Pionirska Street fire." Now, there has been a great deal of evidence adduced during the course of this trial, both by the Prosecution and the Defence. I will be offering commentary on some of that evidence and, in some cases, suggesting different ways for the Chamber to evaluate it. I want to preface my remarks by saying that nothing is meant to cross over into the task that is properly yours. Your recollection of the evidence prevails, not mine, and your impression of the witnesses controls, not mine. There are a number of facts that are not in issue in this case, and it may be helpful to take stock of them at the beginning. It is not in issue that the accused was present when five men were murdered in cold blood along the bank of the Drina River. That is not in issue. It is not in issue that the accused was present on Pionirska Street hours before a large group of over 70 Muslims were locked into a house and burned alive. That is not in issue. And it is not in issue that, on at least one other occasion, the accused was present with Milan Lukic and his men when they committed crimes against some of the Muslims of Visegrad. That is not in issue. What is in issue is whether the accused's presence during each of these events was innocent and just a matter of him being in the wrong place at the wrong time, as he has asserted over the course of this trial, or whether, as the Prosecution contends, he was a member of Milan Lukic's gang of paramilitaries and present at each of these scenes, wilfully participating in the crimes that were committed there. Before discussing his involvement in the crimes for which he is charged, I will begin by reviewing the evidence regarding his relationship with Milan Lukic and Milan Lukic's group. The Prosecution submits that there is now proof beyond a reasonable doubt from credible and reliable evidence that establishes that Mitar Vasiljevic was associated and a member of Milan Lukic's group of paramilitaries. Was Mitar Vasiljevic a White Eagle? That is more difficult to say and not determinative of his guilt or innocence in this case. There was no public registry of the White Eagles that we could bring before you. There were no identification cards that we could have brought into the Chamber and displayed to you. The inquiry that we must therefore engage in is one in which we examine the conduct of the accused and how it related to Milan Lukic's activities and how it related to what happened in Visegrad during the spring and summer of 1992. Let us begin this inquiry by examining what Mitar Vasiljevic himself says regarding paramilitaries. Although he denies being a member of the group, he was able to tell the Chamber in great detail information about the group, such as the identities of these men, many of which were from Obrenovac and not from Visegrad. How was it that he was able to describe these men who composed Milan Lukic's group, especially when others were not? The accused, in his own hand, wrote a list of the names of the people in Visegrad whom he feared. On it, he included the names of several other members of Milan Lukic's group. Recall the several defence witnesses who I put the question to regarding whether they recognised names on that list. Not one recognised the names of any of the paramilitaries the accused had said were associated with Milan Lukic. He and he alone was able to identify them to the Court. There was no other way for him to gain this knowledge unless he had been closely associated with them. Not only did he know their names, but he was able to tell the Chamber that they worked with the Visegrad police. He was able to tell us in detail the clothes that they wore, the insignias that they had on their uniforms. His intimate knowledge of them leads to the inescapable inference that if he wasn't a full-fledged member, he was so closely associated with them to know details few others could have known. But why? Why would this band of paramilitaries from Serbia, led by Milan Lukic, have the likes of Mitar Vasiljevic as a member of their group? Well, undoubtedly his close relationship with Milan Lukic was a factor, but equally important was what he could contribute to the group's work of persecuting and killing the Muslim population of Visegrad. Mitar Vasiljevic could help them identify the Muslims, the houses that belonged to Muslims. It was his function in the group to help them select their targets, and he did this on several occasions. He did it in Musici when he brought Milan Lukic to the house of VG55 and 59, people he knew to be Muslims, people he knew well. He did it with VG115, when he, Milan Lukic, and another member of the group who was not from Visegrad stopped her in the street to inquire about her Muslim husband. No one else in the red Passat that they were in that day knew that she was a Serb or knew that she was married to a Muslim. He did it after leaving VG115, when Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and this other man went around the street to the house of an elderly Muslim couple by the name of Kurpashic. She could hear their screams as they fled for their lives before being executed by the three and left in the doorway of their home. He did it on the 7th of June when he told Milan Lukic where a Muslim family lived as they pulled over the car in Sase, on the way to execute their captives by the Drina River. He did it again on the 9th of June when, again in the company of Milan Lukic and a man from outside Visegrad, riding in the red Passat, they stopped along the road and accosted Rasim Torohan, a Muslim teacher, and forced him into the red Passat, and he has never been seen again. It is also important to consider his disposition toward what was happening to the Muslim population of Visegrad during this period. There is additional evidence that the accused was not indifferent to what was occurring in Visegrad. He, with or without Milan Lukic, was an active participant in the campaign of persecution that was being waged against the Muslim population. The Chamber heard evidence of the accused taking the identification card from a Muslim woman who was simply walking past his house. As she left him in the company of three armed men, he called out to her, "Don't let me look for you." There were other occasions in which Mitar Vasiljevic was seen acting suspiciously, even when Milan Lukic was not present. VG80 told the Chamber how, during the month of June, she saw Mitar Vasiljevic on two occasions from her apartment window in Visegrad. He was armed and in the company of several other armed men, in the vicinity of a garage outside her window. It appeared to her that they were looking either for people or property in the garage. Another witness described seeing him in a car on the road to his house, holding a black flag with a skull and crossbones on it, taunting Muslims in the area with insults, the same black flag, the Prosecution submits, that was seen by VG59 in the Vilina Vlas Hotel, the headquarters of Milan Lukic's group. What has emerged from the evidence of this trial is a clear picture of the accused and his involvement with perhaps the most notorious and brutal paramilitary gang that perpetrated crimes against the Muslim population of Visegrad. In many criminal cases, it often comes to pass that evidence of conduct which is not in itself criminal tells us a great deal about the issues in the trial, and so the same has happened in this case. The accused was standing in the lobby of the Vilina Vlas Hotel on the 7th of June. Under most circumstances, there is nothing inculpatory or even unusual about somebody standing in a hotel lobby, and under different circumstances, there would be nothing about Mitar Vasiljevic standing in the lobby of the Vilina Vlas Hotel, but it is tremendously important in this case. Why? Well, what do we know about the Vilina Vlas Hotel at this point in time? The hotel is closed. It no longer functions as a hotel or a restaurant. It now functions as the headquarters or home base of Milan Lukic and his group. We know that Muslims are being held there. The accused gives us that, but we also have VG59, who was taken there and held. The bodies of young women wrapped in hotel blankets are floating down the Drina River to be pulled out of the river at Slap. It is unquestionably the headquarters of Milan Lukic's group. The only people there in the hotel at that time are either members of his group or their victims, no one else. Now, Mr. Vasiljevic had no obligation to explain his presence to us, to the investigators of the OTP or to the Court. He had no such obligation. But fully aware of his rights, he did explain his presence in the hotel, and now what he has said must be evaluated. One of the reasons he has given is that he was there to pick up his waiter's uniform. I submit that that is clearly just not true. It is not true because his explanation of this so clearly contradicts common sense. He testified that after going to the Vilina Vlas Hotel, he decided not to try and recover the uniform because he considered it improper for a waiter to go into that area of the kitchen where it was without one of the cooks or the kitchen staff. That makes no sense. According to him, the janitor of the hotel is there with keys and access to every area of the hotel. The fact that he decided it would have been improper to get his waiter's uniform out of the kitchen is simply not credible. Now, the Chamber is at liberty to find his explanation regarding the uniform either credible or not. I submit that if you find that it is not credible, you must ask yourselves why he has attempted to mislead you. What is the true reason for his presence there that he is attempting to hide?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm sorry to interrupt, but sometimes I think it's best to ask you the questions when they are relevant to what you're saying. Did you ever ask the accused what his uniform was doing there if he says, as I think he said at that stage, he didn't work there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You did, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And his answer was that his work obligation for when the JNA came to Visegrad was to go up there and serve them their food, and that is why his waiter uniform was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: His second reason for recovering the uniform is equally implausible. I'm sorry. His second reason for being in the hotel at that time is equally implausible. He testified that Stanko Pecikoza - who incidentally is now dead and cannot deny what the accused Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. has told us - he testified that Stanko Pecikoza stopped him on the side of the road and asked him to accompany him up to the Vilina Vlas Hotel to help him find Milan Lukic. The accused testified that Mr. Pecikoza asked him where he thought he could find Milan Lukic, and he responded that he was staying up in the Vilina Vlas Hotel. It is not a matter of the accused saying, "He might be at the Vilina Vlas Hotel, and if he isn't, I have some other ideas where he might be." The accused essentially says: The only possibility I can think of is the Vilina Vlas Hotel. Well, in that case, why does Stanko Pecikoza need Mitar Vasiljevic to take him to one of the more prominent hotels in Visegrad? He can drive there himself, and if Milan Lukic is there, he is there. If he is not there, Mr. Vasiljevic, there is nothing more that he can do to help him. It is important to recognise who Stanko Pecikoza was. He was a high-ranking member of the SDS party, and as such, must have had close contact with Dragan Tomic, the police commander. Certainly if Stanko Pecikoza wanted to contact Milan Lukic, common sense would dictate that he would contact him through the police, and after all, the accused says that Milan Lukic were wearing police insignias on their uniforms [sic] and working with the police of Visegrad. The accused goes on to say that it was his understanding that he was to wait for a while at the Vilina Vlas Hotel and to contact Stanko Pecikoza when Milan Lukic arrived. But certainly the janitor could have done this without Mitar Vasiljevic, and it is certainly clear that no reasonable provision was made for how Mitar Vasiljevic was to recontact Stanko Pecikoza and let him know that Milan Lukic had now arrived at the hotel. We must also remember that, according to the accused, this interaction with Stanko Pecikoza occurs the day before he is to begin cleaning the town. So according to him, he is just released from gaol, is desperately afraid of going back to gaol, he begs and pleads for an alternative punishment. He tells us that the commander of the Territorial Defence agrees and assigns him to clean the streets as an alternative to being incarcerated. And then he would have us believe that he agreed, on the day before this most important assignment, he agreed to wait around the Vilina Vlas Hotel for Milan Lukic with no reasonable prospect of getting a ride home that evening. I also submit that it is unreasonable that the first thing he does when he is released from gaol is not to return home to change his clothes, to see his family, but is to take the ride up to the Vilina Vlas Hotel to recover his uniform and assist Milan Lukic -- or assist Mr. Pecikoza in locating Milan Lukic. I submit that his entire story in this regard is completely implausible and it is the Prosecution's case that what the accused has said about Stanko Pecikoza never happened. It just didn't happen. It is a fabrication calculated to mislead the Chamber from the truth. The truth being the only plausible explanation for his presence in the Vilina Vlas Hotel; that he was a member of Milan Lukic's group and spent his time at the hotel when he was not actively engaged in committing crimes with them. If you are inclined to accept the medical case history in this case, and I'm not saying that you should find the document reliable, but if it is your determination that it is a reliable document, then I submit that you must consider the note made by the doctor of the interview of the patient's wife. If you recall, it says that the wife was concerned that during this very period, she was concerned that her husband was staying on with his unit after his shift was over. Now, when the accused's wife testified she denies having said such a thing, but if you accept that document, then I submit that the unit the patient's wife was referring to was not the cleaning unit that worked for one hour every morning, it was Milan Lukic's paramilitary unit, the unit stationed at the Vilina Vlas Hotel. There is no other reasonable inference to draw from his presence there than he was a member of the group, a vital, essential, and active member of that group. His relationship with Milan Lukic was so close that he was Milan Lukic's essential contact in Visegrad, helping him to select targets and helping him to commit crimes. So essential that he attempted to mislead the Chamber and have you believe that he avoided contact with Milan Lukic after the Drina River killings when evidence has now proven that quite the opposite is true. We have all heard in great detail how his cleaning duties were limited to approximately one hour a day. It hardly seems logical that the commander of the Territorial Defence thought that one hour was -- of cleaning was the equivalent of 24 hours in gaol. It is also improbable that much cleaning could have been accomplished in only an hour. What is plausible is VG89's conclusion regarding his observations of the accused in his cleaning efforts earlier in the day of the 14th as he saw him walk up and down the street with the megaphone without any cleaning implements in a Muslim neighbourhood. There Mitar Vasiljevic called out for volunteers to come down to the street and to clean their gardens. Isn't the truth that one of his functions in Milan Lukic's group was the location of victims through this ruse, through this ploy to trick Muslims who were hiding to come out from hiding and make themselves known to him? I want to return for a few minutes to the incident in the village of Musici because it occurs before any of the crimes charged in the indictment and gives a clear picture of how Mitar Vasiljevic was a member of the group participating in and assisting them in their crimes. Mitar Vasiljevic went along and fully participated in the first night of crimes committed against the people of Musici, and on that night it consisted of home invasions. The home that he went to was that of VG55 and 59. He stood by the door of the house fully armed, guarding it and preventing its occupants from leaving while Milan Lukic searched through it. He even asked somebody if there was somebody hiding in the attic. The Prosecution submits that what the accused claims happened there that night and his view that his presence there was purely coincidental and his conduct purely innocent is simply not believable. It is incredible but for one small detail. He told you that a blonde Serbian woman was in the car him and Milan Lukic that night. The Prosecution submits that this is the same blonde woman whom witnesses saw the following night in Musici when Milan Lukic and his men returned and took nine of the men from the village away, that this blonde woman is the same woman who VG79 saw the accused with as he took a neighbour of VG79's away in the direction of Visegradska Banja, the area in which the Vilina Vlas Hotel is located, Milan Lukic's headquarters. I want to now turn to the evidence of the Drina River killings. Credible and reliable evidence has shown that the accused participated in the summary execution of five men along the Drina River on the 7th of June, 1992. His participation involved assisting Milan Lukic and his other accomplices in guarding the men as well as actually firing into the men's backs and heads until he, like his accomplices, believed that they had killed them all. As the persecution of Muslims grew more and more severe, it caused VG32, as well as other Muslim men, to go into hiding, many in the woods and some in abandoned houses in Muslim areas of the town itself. VG32 took to hiding in his father-in-law's house in the Bikavac area of town. Drawn from his hiding place by the sight of his own car rolling down the street in front of him with its engine turned off, he went outside to watch it as it moved silently down the hill. While outside, he decided to smoke a cigarette. His father-in-law caught his eye with a prearranged signal to hide, but it was too late. He and another family member were caught by Milan Lukic and his men as they came up from behind the house. Milan Lukic, like Mitar Vasiljevic had done several days before to VG81, took the identification cards from the men. He also knew that without these vital documents, these men would be unable to escape the town through its several checkpoints. He was making them prisoners in the town. The men were brought to a house across from the Territorial Defence headquarters, at that time located in the Bikavac Hotel. When Milan Lukic went to find additional Muslims, one of the captors remarked, "Tsk, tsk. What have you been waiting for until now? Why didn't you escape?" Milan Lukic did not have far to go to find additional Muslims. He found VG14 and Amir Kurtalic a few streets away. He brought them back to the house near the Bikavac Hotel. In all, Milan Lukic and his men had gathered nine to 12 Muslim men. Milan Lukic gathered the men around him and made those who still had personal documents on them throw them to the floor as well as their valuables and their money. Milan Lukic made Meho Dzafic go and get his son's car and bring it near the red Passat and forced the men into the two cars. Milan Lukic told Meho's son Ekrem to follow him to Banja, the place where the Vilina Vlas is located. As they drove through the town, the two mosques could be seen destroyed. Milan Lukic told the police or soldiers manning the checkpoint that he had captured some Muslims and travelled through the checkpoint unaccosted. As the captives entered the hotel, they could see Mitar Vasiljevic dressed in a military uniform with a black cowboy hat on. He had a red armband on, and according to one of the captives, had an automatic rifle in his possession from the very first moment that he saw him. He was not the only paramilitary in the lobby at the time, as there were at least two other armed paramilitaries there with them. After a futile attempt to find some keys behind the reception desk, Milan Lukic ordered the captives back out into the cars. Mitar Vasiljevic, armed with his automatic rifle, accompanied them outside, guarding these men who were not bound or tied in any way to prevent them from fleeing. Mitar Vasiljevic got into the red Passat with Milan Lukic. Hasan Mutapcic, and Amir Kurtalic and VG14 were in that car. The remaining captives were in Dzafic's Yugo. In order to overcome their resistance and reduce the chance that they would attempt to flee, the captives were repeatedly told that they were being taken to be exchanged. The cars pulled over on the main road in the area of Sase, and as they stopped, Mitar Vasiljevic pointed out to a house across the road and told Milan Lukic that it belonged to a Muslim family. As they got out of the cars, the calming reassurances that they were being taken for an exchange ceased, and captors, including Mitar Vasiljevic, became abusive and aggressive. The Muslim men were ordered at gunpoint to move in the direction of the Drina River. Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic and the other men guarded them from the sides as they made them walk through the fields towards the river. Mitar Vasiljevic guarded the men by pointing his readied automatic rifle at the men as they walked to the Drina. As the men made their way to the river, some, if not all, realised that they were going to be killed. As they walked the final ten metres to the river's edge, they collected the final thoughts of their lives. On the way down to the river, Meho Dzafic pleaded with his long-time friend and colleague Mitar Vasiljevic to spare his life. Mitar was deaf to his pleas. The men were lined up along the edge of the river. Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and the others lined up a few metres behind the men. Milan Lukic mockingly asked them if they could swim, and one of them asked -- one of the other co-perpetrators asked whether they should shoot the men with automatic fire or with single shot, to which Milan Lukic told them to use single shot. They stood along the bank, Hasan Mutapcic, Meho Dzafic, his son Ekrem Dzafic, Hasan Kustura, Amir Kurtalic, VG14, and VG32. As they stood along the river's edge, and in response to Milan's direction, VG32 could hear the sound of the three automatic rifles being switched from automatic to single mode. One of the rifles being switched was in the hands of the accused as he readied himself to commit the murder of the seven Muslim men. VG32 told the Court, "I heard the automatic weapons being adjusted for bursts of gunfire. That is a sound that can be heard quite clearly on an automatic rifle. I heard very well these three clicks coming from three different sides behind me. Believe me, until this present day, I am often awakened from my sleep by these three clicks." Milan Lukic's gun, a different one, a sniper's rifle, was a semi-automatic weapon and had no such adjustment. As the three clicks finished, Meho Dzafic, Mitar's close friend, was shot in the back of the head. VG14 and VG32 threw themselves into the water and pretended as if Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they were dead. Unsure whether to try to swim away, VG32 pretended to be dead and turned around to place his head above the water on a small shelf of sand at the river's edge. He lay there wondering whether he could more convincingly resemble a dead man with his eyes open or his eyes closed. As he lay there, he saw Hasan Mutapcic, a member of his family, fatally wounded, struggling to stay alive. Mutapcic tried to climb up on the river bank. After closing his eyes, VG32 could feel the wealth of one of the victims as that victim fell on his back. The perpetrators walked closer to the river's edge to inspect their victims. VG32 heard one of them say, "Here's one who is alive." VG32 feared that he had been discovered and braced for being shot. But after hearing two additional shots and a blunt thud as they struck their victims, there was silence but for the footsteps of the men as they walked back to their cars. The two men edged their way down the river to the safety of the western bank and returned to look across the river at the bodies of their friends, lying across on the opposite bank for the next five days. As I said in my opening remarks, it is not in issue whether the accused was present. He has readily admitted that he was. What is in issue are those facts which he denies. He denies that he ever had a gun that day. He denies that he ever shot the men. In fact, he claims that his entire participation in the event was to plead repeatedly with Milan Lukic for the lives of Meho Dzafic, his friend, as well as the lives of the other men as they made their final walk to the river's edge. Just before the men were shot, they were made to turn their backs on their assassins and face the river. There is no witness who says that he or she saw Mitar Vasiljevic shoot these men in the back. The Prosecution must necessarily rely on the common sense of the Chamber to draw reasonable inferences from the evidence that was presented during the course of this trial. The Prosecution submits that the inability to produce an eyewitness who actually saw the accused pull the trigger of the gun is not of significance, for if the Chamber credits the testimony of the two survivors - the Prosecution submits that every indication is they were both credible and reliable - if the Chamber credits their testimony that the accused guarded the seven men and prevented them from fleeing by pointing his automatic weapon at them, then that alone would be sufficient for a finding of guilt. The accused, in his own self-interested testimony, told you that when the cars pulled over in Sase, that he was sure at that point that Milan Lukic intended to kill the men. If you find that, through the walk through those fields, that he guarded the men and prevented them from fleeing as they were forced down to the execution site, then there is a sufficient basis for a finding of guilt. But in fact there is more than that. One of the survivors, VG32, described in detail the types of guns the men had, he being familiar with them from his service in the Yugoslav People's Army. He described Milan Lukic as having the semiautomatic sniper's rifle and the others as having the three automatic rifles that would have been the standard issue for the Yugoslav People's Army. He went on to describe in vivid detail how he heard three distinct clicks of the automatic weapons as they were adjusted just before the shots were fired. The Defence will no doubt rely in part on the observations of VG79, who, from a half kilometre away, had a partially obstructed view of the killing. When evaluating the testimony of VG79, it is important to keep in mind several factors that affect his ability to see what happened when he described seeing three guns fired. He was a half kilometre away, downstream, on the opposite bank of the river. He was observing the scene at an angle. The river bank was not a straight bank, but a meandering one, with bushes and trees growing along its bank. VG79's view of the scene was partially obstructed by some of the growth along the river's edge. It is also important to recall that VG79 was looking at this scene through binoculars, binoculars that he was sharing at the time with another man who was there, and according to him, the other man was the person who had the greater use of these binoculars. It is also important to consider that, when asked how many shots he heard, he said he heard two or three shots. We know from the number of men that died that day and the testimony of the two survivors that indeed more than two or three shots were fired. It is also important to consider that Milan Lukic had a very different weapon than the other three men. His weapon was a sniper's rifle with a silencer or suppressor attached to the end. The suppressor, whose function it was to contain the sound, did this by suppressing the expanding gases leaving the gun. The Prosecution submits that the accused's gun was one of the three guns that VG79 saw discharged from across the river. I'd ask at this time, or draw the Chamber's attention to the diagram that VG32 drew of the placement of the different perpetrators, and that is on the ELMO now, and I'd ask the video booth to please put that on the video feed so that the Chamber can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is this the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. I see it on one of our monitors here, but not the one in front of me, so I trust that you have it before you. If you recollect the testimony of VG32, this is the position of the men that he was able to identify seconds before the shooting started. This is what he saw just as he was forced to turn around and then the shooting began. So I submit to the Chamber that this is the proper positions -- or the proper position of Mitar Vasiljevic at the time those men were executed. He was to Milan Lukic's right hand, he was on the bank of the river itself, and it was one of his shots -- or it was the gun that he was using to try to kill all these men that VG79 saw from across the river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, remembering that the fellow across the river saw only three people, have we got anything in the transcript to show just precisely where those trees were, that he said that there might have been somebody behind a tree?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention, Your Honour, once again to this exhibit. I'm sorry, I do not have it, but if you see, the witness drew very carefully the outline of the trees and the bank, and they were labelled in both B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may not be the same document I've got, but it isn't very clear. That's why -- if you see it's up on the screen at the moment, that's the one that I've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I see some additional marks on this one, Your Honour, that I do not see on yours, so I wonder if that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mine is an exact copy except that it hasn't got the name scratched out from one of the protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your copy, Your Honour, the four circles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The word "willows," you see, and then there are lines there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, by the willows, Your Honour, there are four circles, and the witness had drawn "ML" and "MV" in there to indicate the position of Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the other two are the other two people he said were standing behind him. Now, the person who was across the river was at an angle. That's fairly clear. But I'm not sure what angle it was to this document. They said they were facing the river. If it was straight on, then there's still quite an angle, that the fellow was slightly behind them, who was watching - I think, on the map - who was watching from the binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution would submit if there was a person that he was unable to see, it was this circle that is right at the edge of the willows, that that is the person that he was not able to see. May I suggest to the Chamber there is video of the width of the river. The witness estimated he was a half kilometre away. So perhaps by judging the width of the river, the Court would get some idea of his position and the angle from which he viewed the killing. It's also important to consider that the accused gave his account of what happened only after having a copy of VG79's statement in his possession. Is his account corroborated by VG79 or did he, as the Prosecution submits, adopt his testimony to avail himself of the inconsistency between VG79 and the two survivors of the execution? There are other important issues regarding what happened the 7th of June, regarding what the accused says happened. I will be dealing with those later in my closing remarks in an area of -- when I discuss the credibility of the different witnesses. I want to leave now the Drina River killings and draw your attention to the 9th of June. Now, according to the accused, he was so upset by what he saw at the Drina River that the very next day he went to Dragan Tomic, the police commander and, according to the accused, Milan Lukic's boss, and told him about what he did. He further told the Chamber that after that day, he decided not to associate with Milan Lukic any more. I believe he said it was embarrassing to be with him after what he had done. Incidentally, a claim which is now clearly false in light of what we have learned about Milan Lukic's and Mitar Vasiljevic's relationship in the years since the Drina River killings. Yet two days after the Drina River killings, on the 9th of June, a witness describes seeing Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and another man she did not recognise stop in the red Passat on the road in front of Kosovo Polje. And if you recall, the Serb witness who testified before you also mentioned the red Passat with Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and a person that was unknown to her. The Prosecution would submit that it was the same three on both these occasions which are separated by days. On this particular occasion, they began arguing with a Muslim professor by the name of Rasim Torohan. VG81 saw them push him into the red Passat and told the Court that he had not been seen after this. The very next day, the 10th of June, one day before the Muslim holiday of Kurban Bajram, VG81 saw Mitar Vasiljevic again as the passenger in a green Zastava car on the road in the area of Gajic. He was holding a black flag out of the window that bore the insignia of a skull and bones on it. He called out to a number of Muslims working in the fields, "Muslims, we are distributing Kurban meat tomorrow." The flag was similar to one described by VG59 as hanging in the lobby of the Vilina Vlas Hotel in early June, the hotel where Milan Lukic and his men brought captives and stayed the night. And the 13th of June, the third day of Bajram, VG105 testified how the White Eagles came to her village and gathered all the remaining Muslims together on a truck and took them into town. The people were brought to the fire brigade building. A few days after that, she testified that she saw Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic take some of the men away. Some of those men's bodies would be recovered from the Drina River near the village of Slap later that month. That brings me to the 14th of June and the most serious incident of the two charged on this indictment. The accused is charged for his participation in the burning alive of 70 people, over 66 of which died, mostly women and children, in the Omeragic house on Pionirska Street. For the people of Koritnik, the problems began in early April like they began for many Muslims of Visegrad. After an attack by the Serbs from a neighbouring village, many of the Muslims fled into the woods or across the river to the village of Brstanica. Those who escaped to Brstanica were among those that were gathered in the football stadium, searched, and told where they could and could not go in the municipality. When they returned to Koritnik, the attacks from their Serb neighbours continued, increasing after the Uzice Corps left the area. The last attack occurred on the 10th of June, 1992. At this stage, many of the men had fled into the woods towards Muslim-held territory. Shortly after this final attack, some local Serbs came to the village and told those remaining Muslims that on the 14th of June, they would be taken by convoy to Muslim-held territory. One of them told the Muslims, with alarming frankness, that they were being ethnically cleansed. The Muslims from Koritnik, with no other alternatives, packed their meagre belongings on the 13th of June, prepared food for the journey, and resigned themselves to leaving their homes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The 14th was overcast and there were periods of rain in the morning. The group assembled in the village and left for the bus-stop in the company of some Muslims there. Among the group was Jasmina Vila from Musici, who had been raped and abused by Milan Lukic. Also in the group was a small two-day-old baby that had been born in the woods. The group travelled down to Visegrad when the bus they were promised never arrived. On the way down, they were verbally abused by Serbs both in cars and in the houses that they passed on the way down. When they arrived near Sase, some more Muslims from there joined the group. They, too, had resigned themselves to fleeing the area and were simply looking for the quickest way out of town. The villagers from Koritnik were not the only Muslims who were told they were being ethnically cleansed from Visegrad. Muslims from the village of Smrijece and its surrounding hamlets had been told that they too would be leaving on buses from Visegrad on the 14th. These Muslims gathered in front of the Hotel Visegrad by the old bridge before boarding buses they were told would take them to safety. Milan Lukic boarded one of those buses. All of the men on that bus except one, Ferid Spahic, would be summarily executed at a ravine near Rogatica. What emerges from the evidence is the stark and shocking reality that the activities of Milan Lukic and his men were intertwined with what Muslims believed to be legitimate Red Cross convoys leaving the town. Milan Lukic and his men found that the convoys provided a ready source of victims to be robbed and at times, when they were so inclined, to be killed. As the Koritnik group on its way to catch one of these convoys passing through Sase, another two Muslim families joined the group. Among these ten to 13 additional people was a man by the name of (redacted), a friend of the accused. They, too, had been warned that it was no longer safe for Muslims to remain in their homes. They were also hoping to find a way to leave Visegrad. As the group passed through the next settlement along the road, a small, predominantly Muslim settlement called Kosovo Polje, a group paused to watch the group as they travelled down the read. Igbala Kurpashic, who lived in Kosovo Polje, joined the rest of her family from Koritnik on their way to Visegrad. While these people were making their way down to the town of Visegrad, the accused was already up on Pionirska Street. He was there trying to discover any few remaining Muslims that may have been hiding there. At the time the witness saw him, he was unarmed, with a megaphone, calling to the people to come out and clean the streets. This witness, who was hiding in his attic, explained his interpretation of this curious sight. At this point in time in Visegrad, people were regularly being taken away and being killed. Others were fleeing for their lives, and here is Mitar Vasiljevic, trying to coax people to come out of their houses to clean their gardens and their footpaths. This witness believed, and the Prosecution submits that his conclusion is the truth of what was happening, that this was a ploy for Mitar Vasiljevic to find others like him, this Muslim hiding in his attic, that it was an attempt by the accused to draw them out of their homes. This strange behaviour of the accused corresponds with the activities of Milan Lukic in Pionirska Street a few days earlier. A witness reported that he was up there, telling the people that he would see that they were safe and that they would be secure and that he would help them find safe transportation out of the area. He, like Mitar Vasiljevic would do later, instructed them to remain there and not to leave. What the evidence tells us is that, just as on the 7th of June, Milan Lukic and his men were carefully and methodically searching the Muslim area of Bikavac for remaining Muslims to expel or kill as they had now turned their attentions to Pionirska Street. They were now doing in Pionirska Street what they had done in Bikavac; methodically making sure that no Muslims remained in that part of town. Both the activities of Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic, although separated in time by a number of days, were coordinated and calculated to identify potential victims for their intended crimes. Now to return to the group from Koritnik. The group eventually made their way to the Visegrad Hotel, were assembled and waited for a bus. No bus came that day, and although there are some discrepancies regarding how it was they came to walk towards Pionirska Street, they walked back through the town and up along Pionirska Street. We do know that at least one witness found it strange that, given the many vacated apartments in town, some belonging to a relative of hers, that she and the others were being asked to walk to the last settlement in town, the Muslim Mahala settlement on the edge of town. The group that made its way up to Pionirska Street did so in a long line stretched out over some distance with the slower and more heavily laden people falling towards the rear of the line. Some of the people in the line saw the accused as they made their way up. One witness testified that as she was walking in the opposite direction, Mitar Vasiljevic, in the company of another armed man, tried to convince her to join the group with implied threats and warnings. VG115, a Serb woman who was walking up behind the group, also saw this interchange between Mitar Vasiljevic and VG77. The witness who was hiding in his attic, peering out through the lifted roof tile, could see the group as they arrived in front of the Memic house and disappeared from view between the two Memic houses. Shortly after the group arrived at Pionirska Street, the accused, Mitar Vasiljevic, approached them and engaged some of their number in conversation. He immediately recognised a man from the group, (redacted) (redacted), and exchanged greetings with him. The accused then introduced himself as Mitar Vasiljevic and told the group that he was from the Red Cross and that he was in charge of accommodating refugees. He also told them that there would be a convoy for them in the morning. Now, Mitar Vasiljevic said a number of things to the people from Koritnik and Sase. The Prosecution submits that if the Chamber carefully studies what he said, it will become clear and it will become certain beyond a reasonable doubt that this is when the murder of these people was first considered, first conceived. This was when the crimes against these people began. A consistent characteristic is common to everything he told the people there. Everything he said was intended to trick the people into remaining at the Memic house so that he could go and find Milan Lukic and his other accomplices to commit crimes against the victims he selected. His statements to them fall into several categories, making clear the intent behind the statements and how they were designed to prepare and facilitate the commission of the later crimes. Mr. Vasiljevic knew that these Muslims, just recently forced from their homes by other Serbs, perhaps some already having some relatives killed, he knew they would not readily trust a Serb. They were mistrustful of Serbs. They were attentive to any indication that a Serb might be intending to harm them, and so he began his interaction with them by disarming them of this fear, by making misrepresentations to them calculated to disarm their fear and gain their trust. His first ploy, an extremely effective one, was to impersonate a member of the Red Cross, an organisation that has historically provided safety and security for the most vulnerable of people. VG18 heard him as he said, "My name is Mitar Vasiljevic. I represent the Red Cross. I am in charge of your accommodation and security." By misrepresenting himself as a member of the Red Cross, he quickly had their attention and he had their trust. He went on to further gain their trust by providing one woman there with false information regarding her missing brother. One of the Red Cross's primary functions in a time of conflict is to help family members locate their missing relatives. When this woman expressed her concern about her brother's whereabouts, Mitar Vasiljevic was quick to reassure her, and that he knew her brother was now safe in Sarajevo. He falsely reassured her that she would eventually be reunited with him. Now, once he had gained some level of their trust, he tried to make them feel safe where they were presently. He did this in order to facilitate his commission of the crime. In order to facilitate it, he needed to keep them together, and the best way to do that was to falsely reassure them that they were safe where they were. He asked them if they were settling in in the Memic house and assured them that nobody would harm them there. One witness described him, as saying: "Yes, he shook hands with Mujo and he addressed us too, saying he was Mitar Vasiljevic, that he was accommodating refugees on behalf of the Red Cross, and that we should feel free and safe, and that we should all be in one group, and that no one may touch us and no one would." But Mitar Vasiljevic did not stop there with his representations to the group. In order to increase the likelihood that they would remain together, he offered them false hope, hope that if they followed his instruction, they would be taken away on a convoy of buses the next morning. He spoke authoritatively as if he knew this for a fact or had some responsibility for arranging buses. And if you'll recall, at this point in time, the witnesses were all under the impression that the convoys were being orchestrated and organised by the Red Cross. Mr. Spahic even referred to it as a Red Cross convoy. He attempted to convince them that their surest way to safety was by listening to him and following his instructions. Mr. Vasiljevic is quite correct when he said what could he have told these people about a bus, that he had no such authority. While that may very well be true, it is also true that he made those representations not because he had the authority to but because it served his purpose of holding the victims until he could find and return with his cohorts. One witness, VG85, said: "He said there would be a convoy the next day and that nobody would touch us." The final group of statements that he made to the people gathered at the house were carefully calculated to keep the group together. These final comments were in the nature of directions to them. He had already established himself in their eyes as having the legitimate authority of the Red Cross. He had further convinced them with his statements about being responsible for them and that they would be brought to safety the next day. He now gave them specific instructions to remain together in a single group. VG18 described for the Chamber how some of the people there were intending to stay their last night in Visegrad with some relatives in town. Common sense tells us that if these people were leaving the next morning, they would want to see and spend time with their relatives, particularly during these times, to see if their relatives were okay. Yet Mitar Vasiljevic told them not to, they should not; they should remain together in one group. It was not even enough that they remain as a group in that area. He wanted them in the Memic house. One of the twin sisters testified that when she first arrived at that area, she actually went in the direction of the Omeragic house, and that's where she intended to stay. But when Mitar Vasiljevic arrived at the scene, he told her not to go into that house but called her back and directed her to stay in the Memic house. Finally is the issue of the certificate. Several witnesses described seeing Mitar Vasiljevic take out a pad and write something that he gave to (redacted). In giving it, he instructed the people to show the certificate and that, in showing it, they would not be harmed. He then handed (redacted) a piece of paper on which he had written something. He instructed them to show the piece of paper to anyone who came to the house, including the police. He told Mujo that this was going to guarantee their safety and that nobody would harm them. He also told Mujo to show this piece of paper to anyone who would come in order to be safe. (redacted) then showed this piece of paper to other members of the group. Some of the witnesses that testified before you saw him write this note and give it to Mujo. Others were shown the note afterward, when Mujo displayed it for the people who were inside the house when Mitar Vasiljevic had written it. The accused has acknowledged on cross-examination that he may have written something on a piece of paper for Mujo, but that it was not a certificate of safety but simply his address and phone number. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accused was correct when he testified that he had no such authority to give such a guarantee and that even if he had written such a note, no one would have observed his promise to these people. The question is not whether he had the authority but whether or not he induced those people who rely on his promises, to believe in the power of this scrap of paper, in order to ensure that they would be there when he returned with Milan Lukic. The accused's use of the Red Cross to impersonate its employees and authority was not unique to the people of Pionirska Street. Several defence witnesses testified, albeit reluctantly, that in earlier statements given to Mr. Tanaskovic, they had stated that they observed the accused wearing the sign of the red cross on his armband. Additionally, VG117, a woman who has known the accused from childhood, testified about a day in June when she was brought to the Vuk Karadzic school as a part of the ethnic cleansing campaign in Visegrad. There, Mitar Vasiljevic came, identified himself as a member of the Red Cross, and began to record the names of the 119 people there, who, according to him -- or according to him, he was writing down the names in order to send them to the Red Cross headquarters in Geneva. The witness, in daylight, for over an hour, stood close to the accused as he collected the names of the Muslims. And incidentally, sometime after he left that group, Milan Lukic appeared, terrorised the group, and robbed them, much as he had done before to other people in Pionirska Street. What also has emerged from the evidence at trial is a picture of how this group operated and the tools they employed to overcome possible resistance by the victims that had been selected by them. The tool that they employed was not one they invented and has been used to facilitate criminal activity throughout human history. Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and other members of the group lied to their intended victims in order to facilitate their ability to perpetrate crimes against them. There was evidence regarding the lies that Mitar Vasiljevic told the families of VG55 and VG59. He admitted falsely reassuring them that they should remain calm and that nothing would happen to them, even though he believed Milan Lukic posed a real threat to them. He also misrepresented that Milan Lukic and him were there to search for a killer and needed to search their attic. During the Drina River killings, the victims selected for summary execution were repeatedly told by their captors that they were only going to be exchanged. These men were not bound and could have offered resistance to Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and the other perpetrators. To overcome the possibility of these men resisting or them fleeing, the men were constantly reassured that they would not be harmed and would be released into Muslim territory later that day. The behaviour of the men drastically changed once the cars stopped at the killing site. So desperate were these men to believe the lies told to them by their captors that they denied the reality foretold by Milan Lukic's destruction of their identity documents. Your Honour, does the Chamber wish to break at 4.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We might as well keep to the usual timetable. It might be just as well, though, if we resumed, say, in 20 minutes rather than 30, to see whether we can fit this whole set of addresses in this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume at 4.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to continue with my description of how very often Milan Lukic and other members of his group employed the tool of trickery to help overcome the resistance of their intended victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, all of this is in the document. We're hoping that you might just tell us some of the evidence that you rely upon for some of the things that you haven't identified in the document rather than just repeat what's in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll just briefly touch upon some of the most important ones. Another witness testified to a scene in the fire brigade in which Mitar Vasiljevic was one of the people who took away her father. As the little girl began to cry, he took the small girl into his lap and said, "Don't cry. I also have a daughter. Your daddy will be back. He will be exchanged." And of course we heard in the evidence that her father was one of the bodies recovered in Slap. There has been testimony from Prosecution witnesses and the accused himself that indicates that the presence of the group inside the Memic house was not readily apparent from outside. The door to the Memic house was not on Pionirska Street itself but in the alley between the two houses. There were no fires lit for cooking, and there were no lights in the house. Witnesses testified that the group went into the house and remained in the house. The accused himself testified that when he went past the house 15 to 20 minutes after he left the house to retrieve the horse, there was no sign of any of the people that he had seen there earlier. Yet shortly after Mitar Vasiljevic left the house - and witnesses have varied in their estimates, between 45 minutes to an hour and a half - Milan and Sredoje Lukic arrived with other men. Although not all witnesses recognise all of the people, among the members that were identified were Mitar Vasiljevic; Milan Susnjar, also known as Laco; and Bosko Djuric. VG38 could see both Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic standing in front of the house as he looked through a nearby window. When the men returned, VG13 could see other members of the group gathering some additional residents from Pionirska Street. After the group entered the house, they ordered the people gathered there to go into an adjacent room where Milan Susnjar sat in an armchair with an automatic rifle resting on his leg. He made all of the people strip completely naked and took all of their belongings. During the strip-search, the group from Koritnik and Sase could hear other members of Milan Lukic's group outside the house, laughing. During the course of the ordeal, Milan and Sredoje Lukic took Jasmina Vila, Ifeta Kurpashic, and another young girl by the name of Mujesira Kurpashic out of the Memic house. When they returned, it was clear that they had been sexually assaulted. One of these young women was pregnant. They cried uncontrollably, and they ominously told the other women that their turn would come as well. The men eventually left while there was still daylight outside. The Defence, in its brief, asks the question: Why didn't the people leave at this point? Why didn't they leave after the robbery? What choice did the victims have to go out onto the streets that they knew turned deadly at night? Where could they have gone? They are now at one of the settlements on the outer limits of the town. Their options were to walk through woods that were unfamiliar to them or to return back and walk through the middle of town, a place where they knew it was very likely they would run into paramilitaries. It is unreasonable to expect that the victims could have gone anywhere, and it is inappropriate to suggest that their failure to do so somehow contributed to the crimes committed against them. The group did return, and it was approaching nightfall when they did. They returned in a car that had lost its muffler. There were no lights in the Memic house, and some of the women had put their children down to sleep. When they arrived at the house, they shone the car's headlights into the house to illuminate it. One of the women remarked that they had returned to kill them. Four of the men - Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and Milan Susnjar - each had large flashlights. There were additional men, and although witnesses could see and hear them, they could not readily identify them. Mitar Vasiljevic could be seen standing at the front door of the house. Your Honours, the Prosecution believes it is important to make the names of each individual who died that night part of the public record of this case, and rather than simply read the names, we have prepared two short presentations, the first one which is less than four minutes, the next one which is three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, look, that's the very sort of thing we don't want in a final address. You've given us a presentation during the course of the trial. Now, we've got their names in some document, have we not, already?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what I was proposing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please, this is very important. We've got to know what is the evidence upon which you rely, and all we've got are a number of general statements in this document that you filed as a final brief, many of them without any citation of the evidence at all. Now, that's what we expected you to be filling in. That's what you promised in that document. But all you've done so far is repeat what's in the document. Now, public record. You've got them on the public record. We had photographs. We've got the works. Now, please just get on with your final address so that we can finally try and get from you, when you've finished, the evidence that you rely upon for a number of very important statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Milan Lukic ordered the group to move from the Memic house to another house approximately 50 metres behind the Memic house, closer to a creek. It was the house of Adem Omeragic. There the group was told another lie, that the Green Berets were attacking and that they were no longer safe there. They were also told to leave all of their belongings behind. They were forced to walk in a line between the two Memic houses, toward the bottom floor of the partially-constructed house of the Omeragic family. VG13 was one of the first people to leave the Memic house for the Omeragic house. She saw Mitar Vasiljevic ushering the people to move faster. He actually led the first group of people to the house by the creek. She was only half a metre from Mitar Vasiljevic as she walked past him and was able to see his features sufficiently to be sure that it was him. She, having known him for a long period of time, also recognised his voice as he told the people to hurry up. She also heard Mitar Vasiljevic curse her elderly mother-in-law, who was one of the victims of the fire. As the people were moved to the other house, lights were shone on them from both the perpetrators' cars and their flashlights. Two witnesses saw the accused, Mitar Vasiljevic, as well as some of the other perpetrators, carrying these flashlights. Another witness saw Mitar Vasiljevic, Milan Lukic, and others walking between the two Memic houses, guarding the people as they moved from the Jusuf Memic house to the Omeragic house. VG101 saw the accused as she left the Pionirska Street house. She was close enough at that time to have touched him. She saw him a second time closer to the Omeragic house as she walked close by him. VG101, who had heard the warning that she might be raped, at that point decided to flee. When entering the house, some of the victims were struck by the smell of a chemical on the floor. To some it smelled like paint; to others, like some volatile glue. There were two windows in the room facing the rear of the house toward the creek. The glass in them was reinforced glass. One of the first witnesses to enter that room saw approximately ten other people in the room. VG18 and VG84 were among the last to be forced into that room, and by that time the room was crowded with the perpetrators' intended victims. Someone who VG18 did not recognise shoved her into the room and cursed at her. Over 70 people had been forced and prepared for their death by being placed into that house. VG61's father was probably one of the last ones to enter the room. The people inside, each keenly aware of what lay ahead, reacted differently. Some panicked, others prayed. Shortly after everybody had entered the house, the door opened and Milan Lukic put an explosive device on the floor. One of the witnesses could see Mitar Vasiljevic clearly standing next to him with an automatic rifle, preventing the people from leaving. His face was illuminated by the light from the group of houses across the creek. The explosion of that device ignited the accelerant-soaked floor so that the waist-high flames quickly spread around the room. VG18 made her way next to the window furthest from the door, and as the fire spread, she repeatedly and frantically tried to break the glass window. As she did that, one of the perpetrators lobbed a grenade Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. into an opening in one of the other windows. When she was finally able to break the glass, her son, VG84, pushed her through the reinforcing mesh of the window and onto the bank of the creek below. He followed immediately after her. Soon after VG84 leapt from the window, another young boy about the same age, VG38, also jumped. VG13 saw them jump through the window and could hear gunfire as they did. VG13, the mother of VG38, tried to follow him, but as she leapt through the window, she could see Mitar Vasiljevic shine a flashlight on her while Milan Lukic took aim. His bullet pierced her body and she rolled to the creek bed where she lay unconscious and where she remained for three days. On that night, she did not know if her son had survived nor did he know whether she had, and it would be three years before they would be reunited. The accused in this case has raised the Defence of alibi, and in doing so, the Defence now requires the Prosecution to eliminate the reasonable possibility that that alibi is true. Although the accused had no burden of coming forward with evidence, he did. He produced friends and acquaintances who testified that on the 14th of June, he fell off of a horse and was brought first to Visegrad Health Centre and subsequently to Uzice hospital. Medical records were introduced from both hospitals. In addition to the medical records themselves, we heard from numerous defence witnesses who testified about the records and the conclusions that they were able to draw from them. Finally, the Defence called Dr. Moljevic, who testified that he did in fact recall the night the accused, who he previously knew, was brought into the hospital. The accused's defence of alibi has dominated much of this trial. In many ways, it is confounding because there is compelling evidence that both supports it and contradicts it. It is certainly not the Prosecution case that the senior and respected doctors and nurses from Uzice hospital that came to this Tribunal willingly lied on behalf of the accused. They testified honestly from the information they could read from the various medical records that they used to testify from. While there is still much confusion surrounding the accused's alibi, there are a number of facts which at this point seem beyond dispute. First, the Prosecution, after having some of the medical records tested for authenticity, can provide the Chamber with no evidence that they were in fact forged or altered documents, except for the case of Sredoje Lukic, his name being changed. Secondly, the X-rays taken in 1992 which bear the name of Mitar Vasiljevic and the date the 14th of June, 1992, cannot be of the accused's leg. Thirdly, certain information on the case history form must call into question the reliability of that record. The law obliges the Prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt the elements of the offences charged. It does not require the Prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt every fact related to a case. There are certainly questions regarding how and when the accused injured his leg that I imagine will remain long after the verdict in this case is settled. There may always be doubt as to whether he broke his leg once or twice. There may always be a question as to whether he broke his fibula. There may always be a question as to how he in fact sustained the injury we can see in the 2001 X-ray taken at the Detention Centre. But there can be no doubt that the X-ray of 1992 is not of his leg. There can be no longer any doubt that the X-ray that was part of the medical records of the patient who entered the hospital on the 14th of June bearing the name of Mitar Vasiljevic is not an X-ray of the leg of this man here in court. The Chamber will undoubtedly review carefully all of the expert testimony and evidence in this regard. I would recall for the Chamber the testimony of Dr. Vucetic. Recall, although how it took some time, I was finally able to discover the reason his measurements were so very different from those measurements made by the Prosecution experts. He finally admitted that he used measurements from the lower portion of the tibia to the top, completely separated portion. Common sense makes it apparent that that measurement is of no use because it would change as the bone moved. The two bones were completely separate from each other. You don't need to be an orthopaedist, a radiologist, or an X-ray technician to realise the absurdity of using such a measurement, and I submit that his report and testimony in this regard was a deliberate attempt to confuse or mislead this Chamber. Similarly, there can be no doubt that if the accused, as he claims, always told medical staff that he injured himself falling off of a horse, that the doctor who admitted Mitar Vasiljevic, who interviewed a conscious and alert patient, would not have written down that that injury -- or the correct way in which that injury was sustained. I submit that it is unreasonable to think that a professional medical doctor, after being told how a person injured themselves, would have deliberately falsified a medical document and have written down what we have on the case history, that it was sustained as a fall on a flat surface on the battlefield. Also in that original note was the doctor's conclusion, presumably after examining the 1992 X-ray, that the patient had suffered a simple fracture of the tibia, something we know to be false according to the defendant's -- the accused's own testimony and the 2001 X-ray which clearly shows a healed fracture of the fibula. Your Honours, the accused has no burden of proof in this matter. The burden never shifts from my shoulders. But having said that, once he has advanced a defence, it is appropriate for this Chamber to consider the quality of the witnesses that were called and which witnesses were not called. The Defence had on two occasions informed the Chamber and the Prosecution in open court that it would be calling Dr. Jovicevic, the doctor who admitted that patient that night, the patient supposedly called Mitar Vasiljevic, the doctor who would have seen the person, who would have written that note regarding the battlefield, who would have examined that 1992 X-ray. He was ultimately not called. The Prosecution submits that he was not called because of all the medical staff that were brought before you, this one person who could have definitively answered some of the remaining questions would not have advanced the theory of the Defence case. The Defence in its brief minimises the importance of the fact that in the ledger from the Visegrad Health Centre records from the 14th of June, that those records contain the name of Sredoje Lukic, thereby possibly giving him an alibi to this crime as well. The Defence minimises the attempt to disguise his name by pointing to the date of birth contained in the right-hand column. I submit that that is an unsatisfactory explanation. First, from the rest of the ledger, we know that many columns and spaces of the book have been left blank. It would have been possible to go, to return to this entry and amend it if it were among those that had been left blank. It is also significant that both Dr. Vasiljevic and Mitar Vasiljevic, both kums with the Lukic family, did not tell us who this second Sredoje Lukic was or where we could find him. Or in the event that the name was in fact somebody else and it was amended to correct a mistaken entry of Sredoje Lukic, we were not advised by Dr. Vasiljevic who this person was from the town of Visegrad. What weight you eventually give these medical records and the testimony of the witnesses, you alone will decide. The Prosecution submits that you should be cautious in the weight that you place on them. While the Prosecution has not been able to show them to be fabricated documents, there is sufficient indicia for the Chamber to approach them with caution. Do not do as the Defence has suggested, and that is to summarily dismiss every witness who spoke about seeing the accused after the 14th. I encourage you to carefully consider all of the evidence, evaluate the demeanour of these witnesses and the reasonableness of what they have testified to, and I want to review some of their testimony now. Four eyewitnesses and survivors of the Pionirska Street fire confirmed that Mitar Vasiljevic was present at the time of the commission of the crime, and while it is unclear as to the accuracy of their estimates of time, for a number of reasons, the Prosecution would submit: one, their watches were taken; and two, most of the women that were there were there in fear of being raped and that it is reasonable for the Court to infer that this tremendous fear of such a horrible crime being committed against them could have distorted their perception of the time. The evidence of VG101, 78, 13, and 38 established Mitar Vasiljevic's presence at the time of the transfer from the Jusuf Memic house to Adem Omeragic's house closer in the vicinity of the latter. He carried a flashlight, with which VG13 testified he shone at her when Milan Lukic shot her while escaping through the window. He stood guard as the people were transferred from one house to another. Although it was dark, light came from other sources and nearby houses and the lights that the men were holding. In all four cases, the witnesses saw Mitar Vasiljevic at a distance of several metres. Several Prosecution witnesses who knew Mitar Vasiljevic testified that they saw him after the night of the 14th of June. A day or two after the conclusion of Muslim Bajram, which ended on the 14th, VG105 recognised Mitar Vasiljevic and Milan Lukic when they came to the fire brigade building. Two days after the Pionirska Street fire, on the night of the 16th going into the 17th, at approximately 4.00 in the morning, VG81 was awakened by her neighbours in Kosovo Polje, who asked her to come and bandage a woman. It was VG13, one of the survivors of the fire. On the 18th of June, the day before VG81 and remaining villagers of Kosovo Polje escaped across the river, she saw Mitar Vasiljevic at approximately 6.00 in the evening. She watched as Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic killed a Muslim woman by the name of Nurka Kos. VG81, who lived quite close to the accused, saw him on a number of other occasions from where she was hiding near her house. Shortly after the fire on Pionirska Street on the 14th of June, VG115, a Serb by nationality, observed when passing how Mitar Vasiljevic, Milan Lukic, and two others assaulted a Muslim man by the name of Kahriman on the old Turkish bridge. She reported another occasion in which she saw Mr. Vasiljevic. VG117 testified that on the 14th of June, she was told she had to leave her village on a convoy out of Visegrad. She was told later that she could not leave that day but would leave on the 22nd of June. She and other members of her village were picked up by trucks in their village and brought to the Vuk Karadzic school on Pionirska Street. Shortly after they arrived at the school, Mitar Vasiljevic approached them and told them that he worked for the Red Cross. She stood for one and a half hours in his presence on a sunny morning. His face was not disguised, and she was close enough to have touched him. VG117 described seeing several other people who had accompanied them on the truck, and from that group, she only recognised one man, a man by the name of Cira Duric. She did not know his name was Zoran. A Defence witness by the name of Zoran Duric, in his testimony, would confirm that most of the people knew him as Cira and the fact that he was at the school that date with VG117. Cira Duric's testimony here before the Chamber was clear evidence that VG117 was not wrong when she identified him as being there. Isn't her identification of Mitar Vasiljevic, a person that she knew far better and far longer than she knew Cira, isn't her identification of Mitar Vasiljevic corroborated by her identification of Cira? Perhaps most significant is the fact that, prior to seeing the accused on the 22nd of June, VG117 saw VG18 after she escaped the fire on Pionirska Street. She testified that sometime after the 14th of June, when she was originally told to leave her village, and before the 22nd, VG18 and her son came to the village and recounted what happened to them on Pionirska Street. Perhaps the most convincing is the testimony that was taken from a Defence witness in closed session. I will not say much about it here in open court and instead rely on the confidential supplement to the Prosecution final trial brief. What I will say, that given the testimony from witnesses and experts regarding this matter, the Prosecution has established convincingly that even one of the most important Defence witnesses supports the conclusion that the accused was present in Visegrad and well able to participate in the Pionirska Street fire as described by witnesses. The credibility and reliability of witnesses is always a matter of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. importance, but it is of a special importance in this case. When I use the word "credibility," I mean did the witness tell the truth as they believe it to be when they testified? And when I say "reliability," I mean to say that even if the witness described the truth as they believe it, can we be sure that they are not honestly mistaken? You, the Chamber, will decide which witnesses you find to be both credible and reliable, and return a verdict in large part based upon which witnesses you have believed during the course of this trial. In large part, you will rely on your experience as Judges, as well as your common sense, in evaluating what was said from the witness chair during the course of the trial. I would submit the following for your consideration: There have been a number of times during the course of the Prosecution witnesses' testimony that it was clear that if they were so disposed to testify falsely against the accused, they could have. Early in the trial, the Chamber heard from VG55 and 59. They were very clear regarding the conduct of the accused. They saw him guard the front door and ask if somebody was hiding in the attic, essentially no more or no less. The very next night when Milan Lukic and his group returned to Musici, they believed that Mitar Vasiljevic was among them, but with all candor they said that they did not see him on that occasion. Consider the testimony of VG117. In her view, Mitar Vasiljevic never did anything wrong. She bears no malice towards him. She has not accused him of any crime. If she was so inclined to testify falsely against Mitar Vasiljevic, clearly she could have changed her testimony in a way that implicated him in some crimes. She did not. She merely said that on the 22nd of June she saw him and described what she saw him doing. The reverse is also true. You heard VG55 and 59 describe the actions of Sredoje Lukic, one of the co-accused, and almost commending him in effecting the release of some of the Muslims from the Vilina Vlas Hotel.
