They did not minimise his benevolent actions. Similarly the witnesses regarding the Drina River killings. It was clear and consistent. They never exaggerated Mr. Vasiljevic's conduct in those events. They never tried to ascribe to him conduct which they saw other people do. The witnesses who survived Pionirska Street all readily admitted that they did not know all of the perpetrators. Consider which perpetrators they identified to the Chamber. They identified those perpetrators whom they either knew or who identified themselves during the course of the event. While it is clear that all of the witnesses felt that other Serbs were also responsible for their plight that day, it is equally clear that all of them identified only those perpetrators that they saw there that day. They identified Mitar Vasiljevic, Sredoje Lukic, Milan Lukic, either from personal knowledge or by hearing other people in the house refer to them. They referred to Milan Susnjar because they heard the other perpetrators call him by name. The witnesses had no way of knowing at that time that the accused had worked with a person by the name of Susnjar, also with the alias of Laco, up in Prelovo earlier or at the end of May. The Defence in its brief claims that the Prosecution witnesses have testified falsely before you in order to name a known Serb like Mitar Vasiljevic in place of Serb perpetrators that were then unknown to them. I submit that the exact opposite is the case. The fact that so many of the perpetrators remain to this day unidentified is clear evidence of the credibility of Prosecution witnesses. If they were somehow motivated to falsely accused Mitar Vasiljevic for what happened at Pionirska Street, common sense dictates that they would have also falsely identified some of the other perpetrators as being people they also thought were responsible for what happened to them. The Court heard VG13 testify to all the names of the several men whom she believed were involved in what happened to her that day. In her mind, she believes that the Serbs who arrived to escort the people of Koritnik to Visegrad were involved as well. Given that, if she were inclined to falsely testify about Mitar Vasiljevic, we could expect that she would have included the names of these other men as well. She did not. She simply said that there were men present whom she did not recognise. The Chamber should also consider the costs involved for many of the Prosecution witnesses who appeared here. The Chamber became aware in some instances of the legitimate fears that many of these witnesses had for their own safety as a result of coming here to testify. They did not assume those risks to themselves and their families because they wanted to testify falsely against the accused. They took those risks because they longed for justice for themselves and the people who died in that fire. The Defence has made much of the minor inconsistencies between witnesses regarding clothing descriptions and at times different observations were made. The Defence has put these forward as evidence that some of the witnesses have not been truthful with the Chamber. The Prosecution submits that these differences have an entirely different meaning and, accordingly, the Chamber should draw a different conclusion than that suggested by the Defence. It has been over nine years since these people witnessed the events they testified about. It is quite reasonable that, as time has passed, their memories have faded, that when asked for precise answers to observations that are now somehow vague, there will naturally be differences between the testimony of different individuals. The fact that most of these expected inconsistencies were brought out by questions put to the witnesses by the Prosecution demonstrates two things: First, there has been no attempt to influence the memory of witnesses. The Prosecution takes the recollection of the witness as it has been found and presents it to the Chamber. And second, that witnesses have not spoken to each other about their testimony in an attempt to ensure that their stories correspond. Each told the truth as best he or she recalled it some nine years after the event. The Chamber should also consider the state of mind of many of these witnesses at the time they saw what they described here for the Chamber. Most were in fear of imminent death, some of imminent rape. If we stop to consider the task we give these witnesses for a moment, we can only see how near impossible it is to ask questions like, "Did he have facial hair? What was the colour of his shirt?" At the time, the minds of these witnesses were racing with thoughts on how they might escape or what would happen to their children. This point should also be considered when the Chamber evaluates the testimony of defence witnesses. We saw very clear examples of Defence witnesses who were certain of the same facts as other defence witnesses, such as information about the armband or when they made certain observations. And yet these very same witnesses were so clearly lacking in any clear recollection of other related facts. Eighteen Defence witnesses have applied for and received guarantees that they would not be arrested for crimes under the Tribunal's jurisdiction while they were here in the Netherlands. That is about half of the Defence case. They included the doctors Vasiljevic and Dr. Loncarevic. The Prosecution submits that Dr. Vasiljevic's refusal to treat a critically burned victim, Muslim victim, from one of Milan Lukic's other house burnings demonstrates a great deal about his bias and his credibility. Crimes over which this Tribunal has jurisdiction, there are no minor crimes. What do these people have to fear about coming to the Tribunal? The Prosecution submits that this is a fact that the Chamber should consider when evaluating their evidence. The Prosecution would also submit witnesses like Zoran Duric actually participated in the ethnic cleansing of Visegrad. Or VGD24, a reserve police officer who stood by idly while outside paramilitaries invaded Visegrad, or the other Defence witness who accompanied a convoy like the one that Mr. Spahic was on which resulted in Muslims being killed. I want to now talk about the credibility of the accused. The accused testified on three different occasions over the course of this trial and it is the subject of many pages of transcript. I submit that if the Chamber studies his testimony, it is replete with evidence that he deliberately tried to mislead this Chamber. Sometimes this became evident as his testimony was contradicted by other witnesses. At other times, it is the sheer improbability of what he says that clearly identifies it as false. There are many such examples regarding his testimony. I will name simply seven regarding the Drina River killings. The first is the improbability of the waiter's uniform, that story. I've discussed that earlier. The improbability of this elderly janitor by the name of Susnjar standing up to Milan Lukic. According to the accused, this elderly janitor refused to give Milan Lukic the keys he was looking for, disarmed Milan Lukic because Lukic was rude to him. The improbability of Lukic, and everything we know about him, accepting the elderly janitor's refusal. The improbability of the Stanko Pecikoza story, which I've already dealt with. The improbability of the portion of his testimony that dealt with the cigarette and Meho Dzafic. He testified that while the others were in the hotel lobby, he took Meho Dzafic outside without saying anything to Milan Lukic. It is improbable that Milan Lukic would have allowed this unfettered captive to stroll out of the hotel with Mitar Vasiljevic. It is also not reported by either of the two survivors who were standing in that hotel lobby. The accused testified that when Milan Lukic came outside with the others, he told Meho not to smoke in the car and took his cigarette. Now, according to the accused, Meho rode in the Yugo, his own Yugo, and Milan Lukic rode in the Passat. What possible reason could Milan Lukic have had for not wanting Meho to smoke a cigarette in his own car? Milan Lukic was riding with him, so it wasn't as if he would be bothered by the smoke. There is even a more important reason why you know that Mitar Vasiljevic never went outside to have a cigarette with Meho. You know that because Mitar Vasiljevic told you that he was present when Milan Lukic was trying to find the keys. He was present during all of that. You also know from the two survivors that as soon as Milan Lukic couldn't find the keys he was looking for, he ordered the men back into the cars. There just was never any time for Mitar Vasiljevic to take Meho outside to the pine trees there by the parking lot and to have a smoke with him. It just didn't happen. One of the more outrageous facts that the accused tried to assert was that Meho did not want to be exchanged and that this was the purpose of the accused going to the exchange. He didn't want to go with his son but instead wanted to return to Visegrad so that he could continue his medical treatments at the Visegrad Health Centre. He would have you believe that after being forcibly captured at gunpoint, robbed, threatened with death, the destruction of all his identity documents, that Meho, after all of this, wanted to return to continue his treatment for an ulcer. An ulcer. It's preposterous. The accused testified that Milan Lukic and his men were working with the police in Visegrad at the time. He also told us that he was very afraid of the men Milan Lukic was with. So afraid that he asked not to have -- so afraid was he that he asked not to be made to say their names in open court. And yet he would have you believe that the very next day, he went down to the police station and filed a complaint with their boss, accusing them of a crime. When challenged on this, you will recall he asked Dragan Tomic not to reveal who made the complaint. I quote from what he said. He said, "I asked the commander not to say that it was I who reported it." But recall his state of mind. In his state of mind, or according to what he's told us, he is the only witness to that crime. He does not know that two Muslims survived. He does not know about VG79 across the river. There are no houses where people can see what is going on. In his mind, he can be the only possible witness, and yet it is his testimony that the next day he reported this crime, despite his fears of these men. From the time of his statement in November 2000, the accused claimed that he was cleaning the streets on the day of the 14th. No one - the accused, the Defence, or the Prosecution investigators - realised that the 14th was in fact an important religious holiday for Serbs, a so-called red-letter day, one of the more significant feasts of the Serbian church. Evidence has now shown us otherwise. Consider the improbability Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of him, on such an important day, a Sunday as well, going out to clean streets in the morning. If he had forgotten the day, certainly he would have seen people going dressed to church or hear the church bells. There is nothing to suggest that Mitar Vasiljevic was so industrious that he was inclined to work on a Serb holiday. Recall the testimony of the brandy. The accused contradicted himself when he testified about the bottle of brandy. At first he said that Mujo went to the store to buy it, and then he said that he brought it with him. When confronted on cross-examination with this contradiction, he admitted lying to the Chamber; however, he excused it because he said he was embarrassed to admit that he was an alcoholic and that he had carried the bottle with him. The Prosecution submits that the entire story about the horse is a fabrication and that those witnesses who testified regarding it should not be believed. From the very start, it is improbable that he would undertake this task on a Serb holiday, this mission to save a horse. He was first asked to describe the details of his story in November of 2000, and perhaps he had not given the story as much thought as he might have. Consider the improbability of his intentions: He plans to go and retrieve the horse belonging to a Muslim from a field and then carry it down to the town and leave it alongside the railroad tracks, and the reason he does this is so that the horse will walk along those railroad tracks to a Serb village in which Mitar Vasiljevic hopes someone will take care of the horse. We must evaluate this story in light of common sense, and common sense rejects it as absurd. Consider that, according to him, (redacted) says, "I had to abandon my cows. I would like to give them to you if you would take care of them." And to this Mitar Vasiljevic says no. He says no to looking after Mujo's cows in the middle of the summer when there is little other to do than to ensure that they have water. He ignores the livestock of a friend who lives just down the road from him, yet goes such a great distance and such great lengths to look after the old mare of a stranger. Regarding his account of him riding the horse, common sense should be sufficient to make it plain the improbability that he was able to jump up on the back of this mare without a saddle, stirrups, no bit in its mouth, no fence around to get a boost, that Mitar Vasiljevic, a little bit drunk, was able to walk up to this strange horse and leap onto its back and ride it into town. I submit that it is so blatantly improbable that it could not have occurred. Consider also that the people of Koritnik were all crowded into the Memic house at the time Mitar Vasiljevic says he rode past the house on the horse and could see no one. Certainly someone in the house would have heard the horse, would have looked out the window and remarked to the others that Mitar Vasiljevic was riding past on a horse. No one did because it didn't happen. Perhaps the most blatant attempt by the accused to mislead the Chamber was regarding Milan Lukic's wedding. Both him and his wife attempted to minimise his role in Milan Lukic's wedding by telling you that it was an unplanned wedding, that Milan Lukic simply picked him up by the side of the road, drove with him to the government office, and witnessed the signing of official wedding documents. He denied that there was a church ceremony or reception, and said that he had no advance notice of it. In fact, he told you that he didn't even have an opportunity to change his clothes before going to be a witness. His wife confirmed the story and said the night of the wedding he told her essentially the same thing he described for the Court. But then I happened to ask one of the Defence witnesses about Milan Lukic's wedding, and we get a very, very different account. He told the Chamber that Milan Lukic had a church service, a civil ceremony, and a reception. He further told the Chamber that he received an invitation one month before the wedding. He also said that Mitar Vasiljevic was at the reception and was dressed as you would expect him to be for a wedding.

utterances.text: Mr. Groome, whilst you're on that, you'll remember when that witness, who I think ended up with a pseudonym VGD30, he was shown a video during the course of his evidence in his cross-examination, and he suddenly said: That is not the wedding of Milan Lukic; it's another wedding altogether. What's the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There were two weddings discussed in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but the one that you showed him, the video, when he saw it, he said that wasn't his wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Your Honour, that is not -- the Prosecution never alleged that it was Milan Lukic's wedding. That was always very clear. It was a wedding of a relative of Milan Lukic, where Milan Lukic was the best man at that wedding. If you look at that person's testimony, Your Honour, and in particular, look at it before the break and after the break. Before the break, he's very clear that Milan Lukic -- and he describes Milan Lukic's wedding in great detail. After the break, he's asked a question very early on in the re-examination, and he says something to the effect: Oh, what I really meant is -- I misunderstood what Mr. Groome was saying. I thought Mr. Groome was talking about this other wedding. You will be the trier of fact. I would encourage the Chamber to take a close look at that portion of his testimony, and it is clear that, although he changed his testimony after the break, that it is clear that before the break there was no misunderstanding about which wedding we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, the problem is he actually identified, as I recall, the groom's father, and there was no challenge to his identification of the groom's father, and it wasn't Milan Lukic's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's some confusion here. The wedding video was taken, I believe, in 1997, 1998. It has nothing to do with Milan Lukic's wedding and it was never put to the witness that it did. It was put to the witness, that wedding, because that wedding -- the video of that wedding was sold, in an attempt for money, to a person -- I don't want to mention their name, but that wedding video was sold, and it was just brought out to show that this man had in the past exchanged information for money with Muslim survivors. Now, when we talked about the Milan Lukic wedding, it was at a completely different portion of his testimony. It's completely distinct. And what I'm suggesting to the Chamber is if you read that again, despite what he says on re-examination, I believe that it's clear from the words and his answers to my questions that he's not misunderstanding the questions and thinking that we're talking about the wedding video. It's very clear in his mind that we're talking about Milan Lukic's wedding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's your answer to it, but it hadn't been put in your document. It would have been better if you had dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Your Honour. Your Honours, you may find that the accused has not been truthful in his testimony. You may find that he deliberately tried to mislead the Court regarding material facts in this case. The Prosecution submits that if you determine that if he, or any witness, for that matter, tried to mislead the Chamber regarding a material fact, that you may disregard the entire testimony of that witness. In addition, the Prosecution submits that, in the event that you come to such a conclusion regarding the accused's testimony before you, that you should consider such deliberate attempt to mislead you as evidence of his own awareness of his guilt or his consciousness of guilt. For as long as people have committed crimes, they have also lied to cover them up, to evade responsibility for them. If you find that the accused has tried to mislead the Chamber, then I submit you must ask yourselves why, and I submit the answer to that question is his awareness of his own guilt. The Chamber should also consider that he, more than any other person who testified here, has something to lose or to gain from your verdict. The Prosecution submits that there is a sufficient basis for the Chamber to discredit significant portions of the alibi evidence offered at trial and instead rely on the identifications of the accused by Prosecution witnesses. I want to spend just a few minutes discussing the reliability of the Prosecution witnesses' identification of the accused. You have heard testimony regarding the identification procedures conducted with witnesses. You have seen the actual photo arrays that were used and how the witness indicated that they recognised the accused. The Prosecution submits that the evidence introduced regarding the identification procedures could not have been fairer to the accused and that the Chamber should have a high level of confidence in the results of these identification procedures. It is also significant to this case that the identification of the accused by most of the witnesses was a matter of recognising him from their prior dealings with him and not simply an identification from the crime nine years earlier. The Defence will undoubtedly point to the differences among the descriptions given by the witnesses as a reason for disregarding them. It is important to consider for a moment the difference between recognition and description. That portion I've covered in the final trial brief, Your Honour, and I'm sure the Court in its experience is well aware of the difference between recognition and description. Suffice it to say that the inability of the witnesses to give consistent and perfectly corresponding descriptions of the accused nine years later does not impeach the reliability of their positive identifications of him when presented with the photo arrays. The Prosecution submits that even if the Chamber has a reasonable doubt as to whether or not the accused was present at the time the fire in the Omeragic house on Pionirska Street was started, that credible and reliable evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused was involved in the planning and commission of that crime. It is the Prosecution's case that the crime did not begin when the fire was ignited, or even earlier, when the people in the Memic house were robbed and raped. The first concrete acts to plan and prepare for this crime were those of the accused, when he identified and selected the victims of the planned crime and took steps to ensure that they would remain in a place in which he could find them at a later time. The fact that he may have suffered an injury before he was able to participate in setting the house on fire does not negate or vitiate in any way his criminal culpability for his acts earlier in the day. Your Honours, in the final trial brief, there is a suggestion of these acts and their importance to your consideration of whether the Prosecution has met its burden in establishing the various elements of the crimes beyond a reasonable doubt. I will not repeat all of those arguments now. I would like to say the following: The Prosecution recognises that it has a heavy burden to prove the guilt of Mitar Vasiljevic, and it is not a burden we have shirked but one which we have met with clear and convincing evidence. If the Chamber ultimately resolved the issues surrounding the accused's hospitalisation in such a way to conclude that there did exist a reasonable possibility that he was not present when the match was struck, then the Prosecution's burden must be met on the evidence of his conduct earlier in the day and at a time when he admits being present at the scene. As part of that burden, the Prosecution must establish beyond reasonable doubt that at the time the accused spoke to the people in the afternoon on Pionirska Street, he did so with criminal intent, that is, acts and words were coupled with a state of mind necessary for the commission of crimes for which he is charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll keep going until quarter to before the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is not an easy thing to examine the mind of another and especially not easy after the passage of a significant period of time. Fortunately, in this case this is a tool, a tool in the form of a question, a question that if the Chamber seeks the answer to will illuminate the state of mind of the accused and will lay bare and obvious his intentions on the afternoon of the 14th. I have already described the evidence that the accused instructed the people on Pionirska Street to remain together as a group. What possible reason could he have had for wanting them to remain in a single group? What difference does it make to him whether the group disperses or whether the group remains together? And I would encourage the Defence to offer an answer to this question in its closing remarks. Some of the women there were discussing spending their last night Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in Visegrad with relatives, and this man says, "No. You must stay together." Why? You heard one videolink witness describe how, when she arrived in Pionirska Street, she walked back to the back of the Memic house and was actually on her way into the Omeragic house when she was called back, called back by the accused. Why did he not want her to go to the Omeragic house at that time, the house that was ultimately set on fire? What possible reason could he have had? Perhaps the earliest example of his criminal intent and how it is exposed by this question is the woman who happens by Mitar Vasiljevic and the group on her way down in the direction of town. Mitar Vasiljevic does his best, his best to convince her that she, too, should join the group. What possible reason does he have for her joining the group? Why does it matter to him? It mattered to him because, even then, he had already formed the intent to commit serious crimes against them, crimes that in light of his prior participation with Milan Lukic and his men certainly included murder. In truth, isn't this the reason he drafted the certificate? Not so much to get him to believe -- or get them to believe that he was an official of the town or for the Red Cross, for he had convinced them of that already. Wasn't the certificate his clever way of ensuring that they remained together, that they did not disperse? With only one certificate, any person who wanted to avail themselves of this protection had to remain in the group with (redacted) in the Memic house. Any others who would depart from that group did so at their own peril. By giving them that certificate, he knew that they would in all likelihood remain as a group at the Memic house. Why he did this, we may never know. Perhaps it was to avenge his cousin's death by Muslim forces. Perhaps it was in retaliation for his six-month gaol sentence for illegal nationalistic behaviour in the village of Koritnik. Perhaps it was as simple as trying to impress his kum, Milan Lukic. We may never know. But his conduct demonstrates clearly his intent to participate in the crimes committed against the people of Koritnik and Sase on the 14th of June. Didn't that certificate serve as a fetter stronger than any handcuffs or rope, stronger than any lock he could have placed on the door of the Memic house? Using their own fear and a simple piece of paper, he bound those people to ensure their demise. That old adage about the pen being mightier than the sword is usually used to demonstrate the triumph of good by means of the written word. In truth, Mitar Vasiljevic has demonstrated that evil can also have its triumphs by way of the written word. Using the fear of his victims and a scrap of paper, he bound them to their own demise. He bound them to a fate he had chosen for them. Your Honour, I just have about two minutes left. If the Court would wish me to address some questions, I would certainly welcome them at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean you want to save a peroration for the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you will characterise what it is when I'm finished, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right, Mr. Groome. I'm not criticising you for it. There are a few matters that I would like to raise. The first one is only to clear something up. You did refer to it during the course of your address, and I didn't recognise it until it was too late. The Serb woman who gave evidence of having seen the accused shoot somebody in the back of his head near the bridge, you will remember that she had a driver, and she was asked the name of that driver and she said she didn't want to give it, and as a result of that, as I recall, we said we would not rely upon her evidence of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't recall the specific colloquy on that point. I will rely on the Court's recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My reference is page 1072, but I haven't gone back to check that. But from the summary of the evidence we've got, that's where it seems to be. I just wanted to know whether you had some alternative argument in relation to that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Might I just ask the Court, is the Court inclined to disregard her testimony on that one particular incident or all of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, on that one incident, because she was unable to present the evidence -- well, the name of the person who was with her, for very understandable reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution doesn't have any alternative, and I will rely on the Court's recollection of what happened with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, now, is it the Prosecution case that the accused was never in Uzice hospital with a broken leg during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said earlier - and I think I may very well be haunted until the day I die the answer to that question - all I can say is what I've said before, Your Honour, is that the Prosecution does not have the burden of proving every fact, and I realise that there is still an unsatisfactory answer to whether or not he was in Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. But this is very important to one of the subsidiary facts in relation to this issue of his alibi. It seems to me that we have evidence that you cannot challenge about a number of things because you've tried to have them tested and you can't, and very sensibly you said during the course of your address, well, then, we have to rely then upon the evidence of the people who said they saw him at the fire. But I think it's important for a subsidiary issue to know whether the Prosecution is saying he was never in hospital so that Dr. Moljevic, for example, who had to depend upon the hospital records for the date, that nevertheless he was lying and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems that a couple of things seem quite probable. After seeing the X-rays from 2001, it's clear that at some point he did break his leg. He says he broke his leg on two occasions. You recall that Dr. Raby said that he could only see evidence of one break. It is also probable that if he did break his leg in Visegrad, he at some point would have gone to Uzice hospital. That is the closest major health care facility to Visegrad. When he went there, I believe there is significant evidence that it was not on the 14th. The date that he in fact did arrive at that hospital I am unable to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's why I'm trying to get you to an issue. The issue, as I see it, is not whether he was there but when he first went there. Now, is that the issue which the Prosecution sees?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And if that is so, what is the significance of the discrepancies in that X-ray that was produced by Dr. Moljevic to your predecessor, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The significance of it is that that X-ray which was part of records, the medical records of the person, it seems that there was somebody with a broken leg at Uzice hospital on the 14th of June. There seems to be no question about that. The question seems to be whether it is this man that's before the Chamber. The discrepancy, or the -- I believe what's now been demonstrated very clearly is that the X-ray of the person that was taken that night that presented themselves with a broken leg, that that person is not the accused. Although the name "Mitar Vasiljevic" may appear on that X-ray and on the other medical records generated that night, it is not this man who is before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, the next matter you may have dealt with just very recently in your oral submissions, but it's certainly not dealt with anywhere in the written brief. You say that his state of mind at the time that he handed out the safe conduct certificate was to ensure that they were kept there because there was some evil act to be done to them which you have characterised as murder as a result of his previous association with the Drina River killing. Now, is that the whole of your case on that? Because at some stage during the course of your final submission, you put up some submissions that it didn't matter what the crime was going to be, if he is to be, for example, aiding and abetting it. I don't think that is the law myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I said that the Court understood that way. I think it's very clear that, not only with the Drina River incident but with the other incidents that we've heard about prior to the 14th, that it is clear that his involvement with Milan Lukic is about killing Muslims, and that is why the Prosecution submits that when he intended and took acts to try to facilitate and to try to prepare for the eventual commission of the crime, that he had murder in mind. I cannot say that he at that stage, or there's no evidence that we have been able to bring before the Chamber that he knew specifically that it would be by fire and it would be on such a large scale, but it is clear from what we know about what happened prior to that day that murder certainly was the intended crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm glad that we've got it tied down at last, because I looked in vain for the answer to the question that I posed in that document that was sent to you in advance. Now, obviously you rely upon not just the handing out of the Red Cross certificate. In your final address, you deal with this in a number of places. For example, at page -- I'm sorry, paragraph 340, which is on page 116, you say: "He selected the victims and took definitive steps to ..." I think that should read "ensure" "... they would remain where he left them while he went to notify Milan Lukic and the others and to make preparations ..." I think that should read "... for the intended crime." Now, where is there any evidence that he went to notify Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe common sense and a reasonable inference would lead us or lead the Chamber to the conclusion that at this time we know that there is no evidence that these people are there. There's no apparent sign from outside the street that they're there. Yet within between 45 minutes and an hour and a half later, Milan Lukic and his crew arrive back at the scene. I believe it is a reasonable inference for the Chamber to draw that evidence that, given the fact that there is no obvious sign, that given the quickness with which he, Milan Lukic, arrives at the scene, that he must have been told that they were there by someone, and I submit that that is Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are we not treading on somewhat dangerous ground when you're asking us, first of all, to draw the inference that he went to notify Lukic, and then a further inference based upon, in part, that inference he therefore knew that Lukic was going to murder them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I would disagree with the Chamber. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is a question, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it's a perfectly reasonable inference. Certainly it would be a stronger influence if Milan Lukic showed up five minutes after he left. But 45 minutes is the earliest estimate, is I believe a very strong inference, given that Milan Lukic was not in that area at that time, the fact that he came not alone but with his group, and I believe that it is quite a reasonable inference to draw from that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think we might take the break there, but I'll just tell you what I want to ask you about when you return so that you've got some opportunity to consider it. That document which we sent to you, which I confess to having been the author of mainly, is not as happily expressed as it could have been. We have asked you to provide the appropriate definition of the crimes of, amongst other things, violence to life and person, and then in square brackets it says: "[There appears to be no jurisprudence concerning this crime in either of the Tribunals.]" Perhaps the words in square brackets should have rung a warning bell. What we're after is this: "Violence to life and person" comes from Common Article 3 of the various Geneva Conventions. The Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal has held that that constitutes customary law upon which there can be based a charge of individual criminal responsibility, but in order to do so, it has to also be demonstrated that at the time these crimes are alleged to have been committed there was a proper definition of that crime and that there is -- obviously the only way of demonstrating that is by some form of state practice. Now, the Blaskic case to which you've referred us unfortunately gives us not any clue at all where they got that definition from, and really in order to supply an answer to that question we were seeking some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. assistance. You may not be able to give me the answer when we return, but I want you to think about it and whether you -- if you need time to look, we'd be very happy to give it to you. What we need to know, because we've looked and can't find any evidence of state practice at the relevant time, 1992, which would support that statement in the Blaskic decision that that was a proper definition of the crime. And I'm sorry that I didn't express it very well. You have to excuse me. I'm not an international lawyer, and perhaps I hadn't quite understood what it was I was asked to ask, but that's what we're after. Now, you may not be able to find it in the next 20 minutes, but you may be able to give us some idea on whether you think that you'll be able to find something, because we really do need some assistance. In the end, it may prove to be unnecessary because you've got murder and you've got inhumane treatment and you've got cruel treatment and you've got inhumane conduct, which would probably cover them all anyway, but if you want us to consider that as a crime which at the time of these offences did constitute a basis for individual criminal responsibility under customary law, we want some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a break now until five past. But before we go, Mr. Domazet, we have found at last a window of opportunity, to use a phrase I don't like, on Friday afternoon at 3.00. We can have a courtroom when we can continue. So I don't want you to feel under any pressure to finish by tonight. But how long do you think you will be in your address?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is very difficult --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is very difficult for me to say now, but I think about three hours in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if we start --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: -- two and a half, but really I'm not sure at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we'll start with you tonight and then we'll have to resume again at 3.00 on Friday. I'm sorry for the break. The fire in the kitchen yesterday has caused untold problems with the scheduling, and it's only because there is a trial which will not be proceeding because of the illness of one of the Judges that we've got this opportunity. But I'd like to be able to finish it this week if only for your convenience. All right. Well, ten past, ten past six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Groome, have you got any idea when you might be able to tell us the answer to our problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for not having recognised exactly what the Chamber was seeking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's perfectly all right. It was my fault. I accept that entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask for a reasonable period of time with which to have our experts in international law look at it. The Chamber has said that it has not found state practice. I don't expect that we will have any greater luck, but perhaps there might be some alternative arguments that the Office of the Prosecutor would like to make. If we could have a reasonable period of time to submit something. If, during the course of that, it becomes clear that there is no reasonable arguments to be made, we would notify the Chamber of that as soon as possible. We would not want to delay the work of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I won't put a limit on it at this stage, but I would hope that sometime next week you can let us know how long you'll need.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And then when you've done that, then we'll certainly put a time limit on and then give Mr. Domazet the right to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Judge Janu has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I would like to know what is the position of the Prosecution as to the relation of the paramilitary group of Milan Lukic to the official authorities, army or police or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And another question: From reading your closing arguments, under page 30, paragraph 84, it seems that the position of the Prosecution is that the accused participated in the detention of the Muslims who were later escorted to the Drina River. On what evidence does the Prosecution base its position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Judge Janu, regarding your first question, the relationship between Milan Lukic's group and the official government as it existed in Visegrad, it's clear that at this period of time the government in Visegrad was in a state of flux. The police departments had separated and the SDS had taken control of certain governmental institutions. We know from Mr. Vasiljevic that he said that they were working with the police, and he said that a number of times in his testimony. I think there's also some evidence that we have from other witnesses that show that also to be true, that -- namely, I think the most significant piece of evidence that I can think of that comes to mind most immediately is that as the men are being brought from Bikavac to the Vilina Vlas Hotel, they actually are stopped at a checkpoint, and we've heard testimony from various sources that the purpose of the checkpoint was to check identification cards and control who was coming and going. Not only did they allow Milan Lukic to travel through that checkpoint with these people, but he actually bragged to them that -- he had called them balijas, that derogatory term for Muslim. So he actually bragged to them that he had captured these Muslims and they were allowed to proceed through the checkpoint. The Prosecution would also submit that the Vilina Vlas wasn't some hideaway. It was a very open and public place. The accused testified that is where some of the JNA actually stayed during the course of their time in Visegrad. So I would also submit to the Chamber that his presence in Visegrad was so open, so public, and his movements about the city so open and public that the reasonable inference to be drawn from that is that if he wasn't working directly for the politicians or the police, that they at least acquiesced or permitted him to carry on what he was doing. If you recall, I believe it was the witness Zivorad Savic who testified to seeing approximately 100 or so bodies in the immediate downtown area. So I think it would have been very clear to the legitimate authorities that there was this paramilitary group operating and they would have been aware of what was transpiring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: His evidence, if I may point out, is very unclear as to when he saw that. He said it could have been in June, it could have been July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure if that supports your case, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe there's other evidence. Unfortunately, I wouldn't be able to recite it right this minute, but I believe there are other witnesses who did testify about there being obvious signs, certainly not as dramatic as the hundred bodies, but did see obvious signs of violence around the time of early June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, your second question regarding paragraph 84. It is the Prosecution's position that from the time that these men were brought in to the lobby of the hotel, that Mr. Vasiljevic participated in their detention. We heard about Milan Lukic going behind the reception area and looking for keys, and I think that it is quite reasonable to conclude that part of the reason Milan Lukic was able to turn his back on these people he had captured and to spend some time looking for keys was he knew that the person on the other side of the counter, Mitar Vasiljevic, would keep an eye on his captives. When the Prosecution uses the word "detention," it also includes the period of time when the men were transported down to the Drina River and the period from getting out of the car further down. I think it's important for the Chamber to consider that Milan Lukic is driving the car, Mitar Vasiljevic is in the passenger, front passenger seat, and the captives are in the back and they're not handcuffed in any way; that while Mitar -- obviously Milan Lukic had his hands on the wheel, was unable to watch them or guard them, that the only person who would have been able to prevent them from trying to escape or prevent them from trying to overcome Milan Lukic driving the car was Mitar Vasiljevic, sitting in the front passenger seat with his gun. So that is what the Prosecution means when it says "the detention."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. I just -- I was just thinking that you tried to say - we understood it this way - that Mitar Vasiljevic was present from the beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: -- when the freedom of those people was limited, when they were factually captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. From the period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Not from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: From the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From the hotel lobby forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now you can give us your peroration, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If the Chamber will indulge me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give you the two minutes you promised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has recommended a sentence of no less than 25 years' imprisonment if the accused is convicted of the crimes concerning his participation in the Drina River killings. The Prosecution has recommended a sentence of life imprisonment if you find him guilty of the Pionirska Street fire. To put the Pionirska Street fire into perspective, we engaged in a simple exercise of arithmetic. Assuming that the people who died that night would have lived to the approximate age of 70, we subtracted the age of each victim to calculate the approximate number of years of human life this man and his accomplices were responsible for taking on that night. Not accounting the people for whose ages we do not know, if you add up all those years, it amounts to over 2.000 years of human life. A staggering figure. I want to conclude by describing for you a story, a true story that illustrates the reality of what happened on Pionirska Street. Last June, the Office of the Prosecutor returned to the town of Visegrad to take some of the pictures that were used during the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I hope you're not going to go outside the evidence in this story.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would be just to illustrate a point, Your Honour. I don't intend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But we cannot take into account anything that is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm certainly not suggesting that anything that I'm about to say is evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We were accompanied on that trip with VG13 to show us the places where the crimes occurred. SFOR, concerned about security, accompanied us. When we arrived in front of the Vuk Karadzic school, we left the van and walked towards the Omeragic house. And after spending some minutes there, all of a sudden VG13 ran from the safety of the SFOR soldiers back towards the street between the two Memic houses. A few of us and the interpreter were able to coax her into the van we were riding in. Visibly distraught, she pulled a balaclava that SFOR had provided off her face, and she sat in the van with tears running down her face, saying, "I could see the flames, I could hear the people screaming, I could smell the smoke." Her flashback perhaps is not as imagined as we might think, for, in a way, the fire on Pionirska Street still burns. The hot embers of nationalism that have made that crime which this man committed possible, perhaps even acceptable in the eyes of some, is still there, still smouldering, and all of the water in the Drina cannot put it out. There is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. only one thing powerful enough to extinguish these smouldering embers, and that is justice, a just verdict in this case, a verdict required by the evidence in this case; a verdict of guilty. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I wouldn't like that little illustration you gave to go unremarked upon. I said we didn't want to go outside the evidence. Now, you could only have put that to us in order to put an emotional issue for us to consider about the fires are still burning. It is not really proper advocacy, if I may say so. You're not the first from the Office of the Prosecutor who has done this, and I wonder if there's some sort of belief up there that final addresses can be based upon material outside the evidence in the case, because it can't be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise if the Court sees it as inappropriate comment. I certainly do not expect or ever thought that the Court would be -- the Court's judgement would be affected by emotional arguments. I just put it to the Chamber to illustrate the importance of the Chamber's work in particular and individual cases such as this, that it is a just verdict in this case that is something that is -- or is one of the only things that can prevent something like this from happening again. Whatever the Chamber ultimately decides is a just verdict is obviously for the Chamber and the Chamber alone, and again, I apologise if the Court feels that what I have just said is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say that I do think it is inappropriate, and as far as I'm concerned, I will disregard what you said. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall try not to repeat what has already been stated in the Defence closing brief, and I shall not, at least for now, speak of matters relating to the history and the background leading up to the time relevant for this indictment, because this has not been referred to by Mr. Groome today, and he and I have both referred to it in our final briefs. Of course, if any questions are put about these matters, I will answer them. I will try to focus in my closing argument on the key issues referred to today in Mr. Groome's closing argument. First of all, I shall begin with a contested issue that has been referred to today, that has been considered in both briefs. The issue in question is whether Mitar Vasiljevic was a member of Milan Lukic's group, which was a paramilitary formation. It was not a military formation that was legal. In the opinion of the Defence, it is very important to interpret correctly the evidence referred to today, and this primarily refers to events in the village of Musici in late May 1992; the Drina River incident of the 7th of June, 1992; and the kum relationship obtaining between the Lukic and Vasiljevic families, which has also been mentioned as one of the reasons for the alleged membership of the accused Mitar Vasiljevic in this paramilitary formation. As I have seen in the Prosecution final brief, the Prosecutor accepts the fact that Milan Lukic arrived with a group of 10 to 15 men from Obrenovac or in general from Serbia and that this was sometime in mid-May 1992, this being the time when his activities began. In the view of the Defence, the evidence presented before the Court shows that this paramilitary activity on the part of Milan Lukic and others began around the 20th of May, 1992, when the Uzice Corps of the then-Yugoslav People's Army, or the JNA, left the area of Visegrad and withdrew to Uzice. Although when evaluating the role of the Uzice Corps during the time it was in Visegrad the position of the Prosecution differs greatly from the position of the Defence - and this is something I will not go into now because it's in the written brief - it is evident that in the period leading up to the withdrawal of this military unit there were no significant incidents and life in Visegrad was almost normal. Of course, in the context of the prevailing circumstances, that is, the fact that there were a conflict between two sides all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. Milan Lukic turned up after several years of absence from Visegrad, and according to the evidence on record and witness statements, he spent a few years working abroad. The reason for his arrival and the arrival of his group in the formation that existed is difficult to fathom, especially if we consider that they obviously committed a large number of serious criminal offences, that he and his group were very well-armed and equipped, and according to witnesses, they all had camouflage uniforms, some of which, such as that of Milan Lukic, were blue camouflage uniforms which both then and now are uniforms worn by the police. Others had ordinary military-style camouflage uniforms where the prevalent colour was brown or yellow. This is characteristic because, at that time, these uniforms were not commonly used either in the former JNA, whose reservists had only what is here referred to as SMB or olive-grey uniforms. The three letters SMB stand for "olive-grey" colour. This was a uniform of a light colour, pale green or olive-grey. Many reservists kept such uniforms at home because that was how it was done in the former Yugoslavia, so that when they were called up for military exercises, they could go to the exercises with these uniforms, and also they would put them on if they were called up. Everybody had such a uniform. Let me remind you that Witness VG14 confirmed on the 7th of June, 1992, in Bikavac, Milan Lukic, when searching his home, found such a uniform and took it with him. Mitar Vasiljevic also had this kind of uniform at home as did many reservists. I'm saying this precisely because this is only one of the points indicating that Mitar Vasiljevic was never a member of Milan Lukic's paramilitary unit. I think there is no dispute about the fact and that most witnesses, when speaking of Mitar Vasiljevic's clothing, said they saw him either in a SMB olive-grey uniform or in civilian clothes, in a dark suit or something else, but nobody ever said that he had either a blue camouflage uniform or the other kind of camouflage uniform, the military one, which was standard equipment in Milan Lukic's unit. Not only was Milan Lukic's group well-armed, but Milan Lukic evidently did not want anyone from Visegrad to be a member of his group, and it is evident from the testimonies of witnesses that members of his unit were mostly young people. Mitar Vasiljevic is 13 years older than Milan Lukic. They had nothing in common. They had nothing in common in view of their previous lifestyles. They did not socialise because when Mitar Vasiljevic was still in school, Milan Lukic was already working. When -- when he left Visegrad, there was no further contact between them. The existence of the kum relationship between their families -- when I say "their families," I am referring not only to Mitar Vasiljevic's immediately family, his wife and children, or to Milan Lukic's wife and children, but to all the Vasiljevic family and all the Lukic family. The kum relationship goes back over a hundred years. What this relationship means in that environment was explained by many witnesses, including Mitar Vasiljevic himself, his wife Milojka. And regardless of the fact that the existence of the kum relationship means that there is a kind of special relationship between these people, this cannot be seen as the kind of relationship that would have led to Mitar Vasiljevic joining this group because he was in Musici in late May 1992 with Lukic or in the other event of the 7th of June, 1992. With regard to the event in the village of Musici in late May 1992, it is quite correct, and Mitar Vasiljevic, when making his voluntary statement to the investigators said this, he really was in Musici on one occasion with Milan Lukic. He was in uniform, and he was armed on that occasion. This was the time when he was in Prelovo. He was in Prelovo until the time he was detained and transferred to Uzamnica, which was used as a prison. His stay in Prelovo as a reservist in the military kitchen in Prelovo actually coincided with this period until late May or early June. This was the reason he was in uniform and armed when he came to Musici, because he took the opportunity, as he usually did in that period, to leave Prelovo, in the evening hours when he was off duty, to go to Visegrad and come back in the morning. Or if a van with the driver Vojinovic went to get supplies, he would take the opportunity to go to Visegrad and come back. He visited his home in Visegrad in this way on numerous occasions, as did other witnesses who were in Prelovo in the military kitchen at that time. And due to circumstances, the only time when Milan Lukic came by and gave him a lift in his own vehicle, this event occurred and this is the reason why Vasiljevic has to explain how he came to be in Lukic's vehicle and to have to say whether this proves that he was in that unit. He also testified before the Court that that was the only reason why he had gone with Milan Lukic. He furthermore stated that he did not know that Milan Lukic would make a stop along the way, including Musici, which is on the way from Prelovo to Visegrad. So it was not that they turned to Musici. They passed through the village of Musici. But this is where they stopped. And he went to the houses of VG55 and VG59. What the Prosecutor indicated in his closing arguments was not supported by any witnesses, that is, that Milan Lukic directed him to this house. Mitar Vasiljevic told the Court that he personally knew that VG55 was a member of the reserve police force. He was there for a reserve police officer. And even if he had been at home, even if he were at home, he never said that to Milan Lukic nor would he have ever said that to anyone. Let me remind the Court that the event took place in late May. At that time, he had no reasons to doubt Milan Lukic in any way and fear that Milan Lukic would do anything to harm the individuals in question. According to witness testimonies, the conversation which took place, which was corroborated by VG55 and 59, the subject of the conversation was whether there were any weapons there or not, whether anyone had opened fire on the police which had passed by. And Milan warned them that such a thing should never repeat itself and that nobody risked any harm. It is true that something did occur in the village on the following day. However, as far as Mitar Vasiljevic is concerned, the event itself has nothing to do with him, because on the said day and on the following day, he was never again with this group in the village of Musici. And as Mr. Groome indicated today, this was indeed supported and accepted by witnesses VG55 and VG59, which he took as an example of fair testimony, correct testimony when he spoke about the fact that those witnesses could have falsely accused Mitar but they didn't. This, however, doesn't mean that other witnesses whose testimony -- testimonies I will address later in my closing arguments did not act differently. The interpretation of the story, that is that Mitar Vasiljevic was standing by the door as a guard, is simply an assumption which lacks foundation in facts. Milan Lukic was the one who spoke to the people in the house. He wanted other people also to come to the house so that he might talk to them as well. The fact that Mitar Vasiljevic did not want to enter the house was explained by him. He stated that he didn't think that his presence inside the house was necessary, that he simply remained standing there. And as to the doubt which had been expressed regarding the presence of anyone in the house or in the attic, he personally asked the witness whether this was correct or not, and when the witness said that it was not, he told Milan Lukic that that was true, that the man was telling the truth. Maybe it was in this way that he wanted to avoid any uncomfortable situation or Milan Lukic searching the house. It is true that he found himself in a situation that he perhaps didn't want to find himself in because he knew these people personally, and these people knew him very well too. His presence in the village on the said night only involved these facts. He left the village without knowing that what transpired later on and what was discussed later on by witnesses. VG55 and VG59 didn't know the fact that other villagers remained in the house and that other members of Milan Lukic's paramilitary unit robbed the house in the meantime. This, I believe, is reproached to Mitar Vasiljevic in the Prosecutor's final brief. It is alleged he should have noticed that and that he should have been aware of that fact and that that would prove his participation in the events. However, that is not what follows from the evidence, because this was not known by the witnesses who were at the house at that time, in the house where Milan Lukic was and at whose door Mitar Vasiljevic stood. They left the place in their vehicle as they had left Prelovo earlier on, and nothing happened on that evening, nothing that would have caused Mitar Vasiljevic to believe that anything untoward would happen the following day. However, the fact that he appeared in the village of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Musici on that night with Milan Lukic can by no means constitute evidence as to his membership in his paramilitary formation, because at that time, and that is something which was testified by Defence witnesses such as Vojinovic, Lindo, Simic, who stated that throughout that period of time they were at the military kitchen and that Mitar Vasiljevic was also present at all times in the military kitchen except on those occasions when he went home to see his family or when he went to Visegrad to get the supplies. This was one such occasion. He took the opportunity of having transport home, and he happened by chance to be in the village of Musici, which is, I have to state once again, situated on the very road leading from Prelovo to Visegrad to the Vasiljevic house which is situated on the same road in the outskirts of Visegrad. Therefore, it is our submission, Your Honours, that Mitar Vasiljevic's presence there, which was not in itself disputed by the Defence, cannot constitute evidence about his membership in Milan Lukic's group. Let me now move to the second event which is interpreted once again as evidence of his membership in Milan Lukic's group, namely the Drina River incident which took place on the 7th of June, 1992. There was a lot of talk in the closing arguments that we heard today about the fact that Mitar Vasiljevic did not happen to be at the hotel accidentally. Assertions would made that the hotel was Milan Lukic's base and that the reasons for that was not Pecikoza's story or he's going to take the -- his uniform which was in the hotel but that he was there to help out Milan Lukic. Let me now focus on certain details which dispute the assumption made by the Prosecution. Had that been one of -- that that was one of the bases of Milan Lukic we can perhaps accept as true because there have been several cases detention of various people in the hotel even before that. The hotel was not used as a hotel during that period of time. However, let me remind you of the fact that Milan Lukic came to the hotel with two of his soldiers and seven Muslims. He was approached first of all by an individual wearing camouflage uniform, who told him, "This stupid person has released your detainees," referring to Susnjar, who was an employee of the hotel, who worked at the hotel. He wanted explanation from Susnjar, and he allegedly asked Susnjar for the keys to one of the rooms. It is also alleged that Mitar Vasiljevic was standing in the lobby near the passage leading to the swimming pool, which was explained by Witness VG42. Nobody asked him anything. Nobody requested anything from him. That Mitar Vasiljevic -- it is alleged that Mitar Vasiljevic was there as a member of the group, that he guarded the prisoners. Of course, we believe that it would have been normal for Milan Lukic to address him first of all and to talk to him before anyone else, especially in view of the fact that their kum relationship is being so emphasised. But it is because of the way the events unfolded and because of the way this conversation proceeded, it is obvious that Mitar Vasiljevic had nothing to do with what happened. It is our submission that he had nothing to do with the release of the detainees, the release in respect of which explanation had been asked from Susnjar, and that he talked to one of the members of this group. Explanation was given that the people had been detained for several days and that Milan was not there and that that was the reason why the individuals were released. Milan Lukic, it follows from the evidence, was absent from the Vilina Vlas Hotel for several days. It is therefore not credible that Mitar Vasiljevic should have known that, that he should have come there without knowing that Milan Lukic was there or not. Let me remind you of the fact that the day before that, Mitar Vasiljevic attended the funeral of his cousin in the village of Vardiste, together with his wife, which event occurred on a Saturday, which was the 6th of June, that he had already visited the family to express his condolences, which took place after his release from prison. Mr. Groome, in his argument, used this particular fact to allege that it would not have been logical for Mitar Vasiljevic to do so the day before he started his cleaning duties, that is, that it would not have been logical for him to go to the Vilina Vlas Hotel with Stanko Pecikoza to look for Milan Lukic. It is not true that he was supposed to start cleaning the city on that day. He had already started with his cleaning duties. They began on the day of his release from prison and not on that particular day. It was not on that particular day that he was released from prison, because that would have been the 6th or the 7th of June, and you can find, Your Honours, this in our brief. He was released from prison on or about the 3rd of June, maybe even a day before that date, because obviously this release was linked to his learning about his cousin's death. And in view of the fact that he remained two or three days in prison only, that could have only taken place at the very beginning of June, that is, on the 1st, the 2nd, or the 3rd of June. Prior to the funeral, he had gone to Vardiste on one occasion, and then on the 6th of June, on Saturday, he went to the funeral. The event in question took place on the 7th of June. The allegation that nobody spoke to Mitar Vasiljevic at the reception of the Vilina Vlas Hotel -- the fact - excuse me - the fact that nobody spoke to Mitar Vasiljevic at the reception of the Vilina Vlas Hotel follows from the evidence given by VG14 and VG32. They told the Court that he had stayed there, that he didn't say a word throughout that period of time, whilst Milan Lukic was being very angry at Susnjar. He was looking for the keys, and he was coming and going, and eventually he ordered everyone to go back and to take the car and to return to where they had come from. That is, the fact that Mitar Vasiljevic happened to be, on the 7th of June, in this manner, that he happened to be there on that particular day, can by no means constitute evidence of his membership in Milan Lukic's unit, especially in view of the submission made by Mr. Groome today that it is absolutely unacceptable that he came to the hotel for the reason that he had stated. It is my submission, Your Honour, that what he said is correct and true. Stanko Pecikoza was indeed a highly ranking Serb official within the SDS party, as was stated by the Prosecutor today, but he was also a man who protected Muslims. He was also a very good friend of Mitar Vasiljevic. Mitar Vasiljevic even worked at his place - he made some woodwork in his house - and he had no reason to refuse his request, that is, when he wanted to go and see -- go and find Milan Lukic. Although at first sight it may seem unnecessary or illogical, however, the truth is that he simply did not refuse that request. And the uniform was a subsidiary issue, and he believed that it would be a good opportunity for him to take the uniform from the hotel.

utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, we'll resume again at 3.00 on Friday. I don't know which courtroom we'll be in, but you'll be notified. 3. Well, let's hope that it's been repaired from the fire. But when you do resume, Mr. Domazet, please remember: We have read your submissions. We don't want the evidence simply repeated. You're here to argue further matters and to respond to Mr. Groome's arguments, but we don't want you just simply to tell us what's already in the document, which we've read. 3.00 on Friday.
